subtopic: PACIFIC COAST LONGSHOREMEN DISPUTE-PERSONNEL OF INDUSTRIAL INQUIRY

speakeroldname: Hon. J. R. Nicholson (Minister of Labour):
subtopic: PACIFIC COAST LONGSHOREMEN DISPUTE-PERSONNEL OF INDUSTRIAL INQUIRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last week I announced in the house that, as part of the understanding that resulted in the resumption of operations in the British Columbia ports, an industrial inquiry commission would be appointed to investigate the causes of the stoppage, which has paralysed ports for so long and with such far-reaching adverse effects, also to make recommendations with respect to the avoidance of similar situations in future, and with respect to the undertaking for the consideration of the grievances of foremen.
I now wish to announce the appointment of Mr. Justice C. Rhodes Smith of the Court of Appeal of Manitoba as the industrial inquiry commissioner. As I am sure hon. members are aware, Mr. Justice Smith is a former minister of labour of the province of Manitoba and he served with distinction for a number of years as chairman of the Canada Labour Relations Board.
I am also pleased to announce that Mr. Justice Smith will be assisted by two assessors. One of these is Captain H. J. C. Terry, retired, of Vancouver, the former president of Northland Navigation Company Limited, who, since his retirement, has done such excellent work as president of the Pacific National Exhibition over the past few years. The other assessor is Mr. Joseph Morris, executive vicepresident of the Canadian Labour Congress, who is well known and highly respected in all parts of Canada, especially on the west coast where he served with such distinction as president of the International Woodworkers Association before coming to Ottawa.
I am also pleased to announce that, pursuant to the amendments to the Canada Labour (Standards) Code, to which royal assent was given late yesterday, an order in council has been passed today establishing regulations governing holiday pay for longshoremen for the eight statutory holidays. It is expected that the regulations governing annual vacations for longshoremen will be promulgated in the very near future.

speechtext: should like to address a question to the Prime Minister with reference to the announcement that Canada is to be a member of the seven man committee to plan the nuclear strategy in NATO. Does acceptance of this responsibility involve repudiation of the pledge the Prime Minister made three years ago to negotiate Canada out of its nuclear role?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: NATO-PARTICIPATION BY CANADA IN NUCLEAR PLANNING
speechtext:
No, Mr. Speaker. Up to the establishment of this committee, nuclear planning matters had been dealt with by the NATO council as a whole. It is true that yesterday a nuclear planning group was set up as part of the NATO machinery, which will consist of seven members, including Canada, who will serve for an initial period of 18 months. At the end of that time certain members of the group will be replaced.
The purpose of the group is related to planning for nuclear defence of the alliance. It will permit broadened participation by member countries in making recommendations to the council on these matters.
The concept of a broadened participation by the members of the alliance is an important development for many reasons, not the least of which is the prospect it may advance international efforts to achieve an effective world wide non-proliferation agreement. It should be emphasized, Mr. Speaker, that membership in this group in no way increases Canada's involvement in nuclear matters. The

establishment of nuclear planning machinery is simply a more efficient way of dealing with a problem which, in any event, would come before the council.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Prime Minister of which I have given him notice. Has the Canadian government made any representations to the governments in Washington and Hanoi with regard to the extension of the Christmas truce in the hostilities in Viet Nam along the lines proposed by His Holiness the Pope and the Secretary General of the United Nations?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank my hon. friend for having given me notice of his question. The government has welcomed, as I am sure have all hon. members of the house, the decision to institute truces in the war in Viet Nam at Christmas and the New Year, and the proposal for a further truce at the lunar new year in February. The possibility of prolonging these truces and making them the basis for introducing an element of reducing and ending hostilities is one which we earnestly hope the parties to the conflict will consider very seriously, as it is an important preliminary step toward peace. It is with this possibility in mind that we have welcomed, as I am sure the house welcomes, the spirit in which His Holiness the Pope and the Secretary General have issued their appeals.
I have seen news reports from Washington this morning, as my hon. friend may have, which indicate that the United States government would be willing to discuss, if I may quote from one particular report, "a prolonged cease fire or any other reduction in the fighting in Viet Nam in direct negotiation with the communist side". That is the end of the quotation from the report.
I am sure that I speak for all members in expressing the hope that some comparable indication will be forthcoming from the other side. Canada's views on this problem, Mr. Speaker, are well known to the capitals concerned. These views have also been discussed with the Pope and the Secretary General of the United Nations.
Beyond that, Mr. Speaker, I can only say that if there is any helpful role that we can play in relation to a possible cease fire, either individually or as a member of the international commission, we would be only too happy to have the privilege of doing this.

speechtext: Order. When the committee rose at the last sitting, clause 1 was being discussed. Shall clause 1 carry?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare; Minister of Amateur Sport
subtopic: PROVISION OF GUARANTEED INCOME SUPPLEMENT AND DETERMINATION OF PENSIONERS' INCOMES
speechtext:
Yes, I have been in touch with my colleague, the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. My officials have also had an opportunity to discuss this question with the officials of the other department. It appears that the number of Indians receiving supplementation of old age security pensions through extra payments from the department is not great and we expect that generally the great majority of the pensioned Indian population will be better off as a result of pension supplements.
In cases where the amount of $105 is not enough to meet the requirements of Indian pensioners, the department of Indian affairs will be prepared to pay additional assistance. We think the number of cases involved will be small, and that those mainly affected will be Indians in need of special care living off the reservations.

subtopic: PROVISION OF GUARANTEED INCOME SUPPLEMENT AND DETERMINATION OF PENSIONERS' INCOMES
speechtext:
The minister has told us that in his opinion the great majority of Indians receiving old age pensions, those who will be receiving the $105 a month, will be better off under this legislation. I agree that this may be the case. Nevertheless, in my opinion $105 a month is not enough for an old age pensioner living in an isolated area, bearing in mind the extremely high cost of living in such areas. And most of the people I am concerned about now do live in isolated areas. I happen to know that a great many Indian old age pensioners are receiving very little more than their $75 a month. The department has undoubtedly felt that $75 a month is sufficient. I say it is not.
In any case, it appears to me that the minister is not able to assure us that any of the pensioners who are now receiving supplementary assistance from the Indian Affairs branch, in addition to the $75 a month, will continue to receive assistance supplementary to the extra $30 a month they may be receiving.
I can understand the hon. gentleman's difficulty when it comes to giving such an
Old Age Security Act Amendment assurance. But I should like to point out to him that if the federal government, which controls the department concerned, cannot give this committee an assurance that supplementary payments will be continued, it is setting a precedent for the provinces; faced with such an example, the provinces will be considering very closely the idea of decreasing their own supplementary payments to recipients of old age pensions. This is what I am afraid will happen. I do not think there is much hope that the provinces will continue to make these supplementary payments unless the federal government itself can assure the committee that it intends to take the initiative and continue this class of payments to old age pensioners among our Indian people.

subtopic: PROVISION OF GUARANTEED INCOME SUPPLEMENT AND DETERMINATION OF PENSIONERS' INCOMES
speechtext:
I have two minor points. When we come to later clauses dealing with the application of this measure, we shall be asking some questions about the type of application which may be imposed.
I understand a draft application form has been prepared. Would the minister make copies of it available to us? We recognize it would merely be a starting point, but it would give us some idea of the type of application form which may be necessary for the purposes of this bill.
Second, has the minister consulted with the Minister of Veterans Affairs as to the possibility that the supplementary payment made under this amendment would not be considered as income for the purposes of war veterans allowance? I recognize that payment of war veterans allowance is not considered as income for the purposes of this bill, but it may work the other way around. The receipt of a possible $30 under this bill might prejudice the war veterans allowance payment.

subtopic: PROVISION OF GUARANTEED INCOME SUPPLEMENT AND DETERMINATION OF PENSIONERS' INCOMES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, last Monday the minister and I were just commencing a very interesting discussion with regard to certain questions which could arise as to the legality of this legislation, having in mind certain actions which might be taken by certain provinces. Since then I have reviewed Hansard, including the discussion initiated by the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi, the speech made by the hon. member for Sherbrooke and the statement made by the minister in response to questions which I asked him.
I have too much respect for the minister as a good parliamentarian not to feel that his answer to me was carefully phrased to avoid answering very important questions, and I

December 15, 1966

Old Age Security Act Amendment believe this bill should not be passed until we receive some better answers.
I have taken the position throughout, Mr. Chairman, that the responsibility of the federal government should be exercised in respect of subject matters which are essential to make the central government strong and viable. I have always supported the government in its efforts in that regard, but here we have something entirely different. Here we are getting into the twilight area, the gray zone between federal and provincial governments.
It is all very well for the minister to say to me, and quite correctly, that as matters now stand the government has a legal opinion to the effect it is entitled to enact legislation of this kind. I accept that fact. There is no doubt about it, but I am looking to what the situation will be respecting this legislation in the event that a province, as one province has already indicated, enacts legislation of a similar kind.
I can do no better, for the purposes of the record, than put the very brief provision of section 94A of the British North America Act on record at this point. It reads:
It is hereby declared that the Parliament of Canada may from time to time make laws in relation to old age pensions in Canada, but no law made by the Parliament of Canada in relation to old age pensions shall affect the operation of any law present or future of a provincial legislature in relation to old age pensions.
It is notorious that this section was enacted in 1951, after several abortive attempts had been made to give to the federal government exclusive jurisdiction in this particular matter. In 1964, when the government secured the constitutional amendments providing for supplementary benefits, in the form of survivor and disability clauses, I brought this matter up in the house. I asked the Prime Minister a question in June, 1964. I asked why the government at that time, when securing a constitutional amendment, did not attempt to secure the exclusive right to deal with old age pensions and matters of this description.
I did not get any answer, but in the course of the debate which followed, when the address was presented by the Prime Minister, I again brought this matter to the attention of the government and the Prime Minister. I referred to the fact that when the first amendment was introduced in 1951, as originally proposed by hon. Mr. Garson, at that time the minister of justice, it was on a very simple basis. It was to the effect that notwithstanding anything in the British North America Act,


the parliament of Canada may make laws in relation to old age pensions.
That was the orignial proposal of the federal government but the provinces would not accept it, for reasons which they thought adequate. So, as a result of discussions and correspondence between the premiers and the federal government, a condition was added which was, as I have just read, that "no law made by the parliament of Canada in relation to old age pensions shall affect the operation of any law present or future of a provincial legislature. . ."
The current situation has been inflamed by events. We have seen the introduction of a statement into the Quebec legislature that it is their intention to enact old age pension laws. What then will be the position of this legislation here? Let us assume-and it is not at all unlikely-that the type of legislation which the province of Quebec, or any other province, may introduce will establish certain age limits which may differ from the age limits in this legislation. They may establish in their legislation different amounts. They may establish in their legislation different conditions of payment and sources of funds.
Surely, under those conditions it cannot be successfully argued that the continued attempt to implement the provisions of this, and the original legislation upon which it is based, will not have the effect of interfering with the operation of a provincial act dealing with old age pentions? I am not going to follow this line of argument, nor is this the place to do so, through to its completion. But, Mr. Chairman, I suggest this is a very real possibility and so, while the minister was quite correct on Monday when he said the government has every legal right to enact this legislation-and that is a statement with which I wholeheartedly agree-this will not necessarily be the case when the province of Quebec, or any other province if it so sees fit, exercises its constitutional responsibility to deal with matters of this kind. The likely result of the operation of this federal legislation will be to interfere with the operation of the provincial legislation.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
What is the government going to do then? What will be the position of the pensioners? What about the sources of funds? What about the old age security fund? These are matters with which the government must be concerned, and it is not for the minister to fob off the committee with the casual statement
December 15, 1966	COMMONS
which he made on Monday. It is a very difficult problem.
The minister may well say in reply to my comments that this is all theoretical, that it is all hypothetical, but in the light of the statement in the speech from the throne in the Quebec legislature, it is getting to be more than theoretical. I think the members of this committee are entitled to some indication as to what the views of the government are, not as the situation is today but as it may well be if such an event comes about.
Before I resume my seat I make this suggestion to the minister, that he might well give serious consideration to the provisions of the Supreme Court Act. There is a very simple and adequate remedy under, I believe, section 55, where the Governor in Council has the right to submit to the Supreme Court references not only as to existing legislation but as to the powers of either the legislature of any province or of the federal government which have been exercised or which may be exercised.
I suggest to the minister that if it does become apparent that specific legislation is going to be introduced in the province of Quebec then there is a duty incumbent upon this government to seek, through the medium of the Supreme Court Act, an opinion of the Supreme Court of Canada as to what would be the situation. I put this suggestion quite sincerely to the minister. I suggest the government should not leave this question until the last, until we have in existence legislation of a province and this legislation of the federal government, which are in direct conflict. There is very grave doubt as to whether or not this legislation, which we are now being asked to enact, is in fact valid in view of the possible operation of provincial legislation.

subtopic: PROVISION OF GUARANTEED INCOME SUPPLEMENT AND DETERMINATION OF PENSIONERS' INCOMES

Mr. Chairman, under this proposed measure, we define income as it is defined in the Income Tax Act. In addition to those items which have been mentioned by the hon. member for Churchill we would not regard, for example, unemployment insurance benefits as income for purposes of this supplement; nor would we regard as income payment for workmen's compensation or any form of social assistance including war veterans' allowances; nor would we consider as income disability pensions received by veterans with regard to war service or indeed pensions in a form which in a sense is an award for damages.
These are among the additional items which are not included which come to mind immediately. We do not include donations or gifts from relatives or friends. Old age pensioners receiving gifts from their children, for example, would not be expected to regard these as income. As you may remember the Senate committee recommended that all cash income be regarded as income for the purposes of the program, but we have not accepted that definition. We have accepted the definition of income as provided by the Income Tax Act and, accordingly, we have knocked out quite a number of items which otherwise might have been included, if the Senate conclusion had been accepted.

The pension payment
made in Prince Edward Island was considered. In proposed section 9, as contained in clause 3, there is a provision that the amount of any pension or supplement and the amount of any similar payment under a law of the legislature of a province shall not be regarded as income. Therefore, if an applicant from Prince Edward Island applied for this guaranteed income supplement such an applicant would not have to put down on the application form as income the $25 of the P.E.I. pension payment. It is then up to the province to do what it wishes to do. We do not, however, disqualify any pensioner from receiving this benefit by virtue of a supplement received from a province.

subtopic: PROVISION OF GUARANTEED INCOME SUPPLEMENT AND DETERMINATION OF PENSIONERS' INCOMES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think the proposition which has been advanced here this afternoon dealing with the constitutional position in respect to old age pension legislation must be answered by the government. That the government should sit in solitary splendour and look on while a question of such importance is raised is something which cannot be accepted by this house. Indeed, it is quite amazing to me, as I read my correspondence from day to day, the number of people who write to me and say, "Well now, what stand is being taken on behalf of a straight pension to all Canadians in view of the fact that each Canadian who pays income tax, corporation tax, and the like, has made a contribution which entitles him to a pension".
No longer is there any suggestion in legislation of this kind that what is being granted is in the nature of an emolument or benefit. Today it constitutes an earned income in consequence of contributions made by all Canadians. I should like to make clear once more that our attitude has been, and still is, that what is being done here by the government is unjust and unfair, and that all

Canadians who are entitled to the old age pension should receive the amount of the pension which we continually and regularly have advocated should be $100 a month.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
What is perpetrated by this legislation is a departure from a principle established and accepted by Canadians as a whole, that everyone should be entitled to the same pension regardless of his or her circumstances. The argument that a means test should be applied today is one that cannot be accepted. This is simply a step backwards, as has been said over and over again during the course of this debate, and is detrimental to human dignity. No matter what attitude the government adopts, what is being done here is an application of the means test. The government tries to dignify it by calling it another name, but a rose by any other name is just as sweet and a thorn by any other name is just as "Sharp". This is without doubt an economic and political gimmick, because we are departing from a principle which has been accepted over the years.
I am not going to go into detail in respect of this matter as it has been dealt with fully by other hon. members, but I should like to point out again that the opposition has repeatedly moved amendments, in an endeavour to recruit the support of members on the government side, to increase pensions to $100 per month. We went as far as to suggest that a vote on such an amendment would not be considered a vote of non-confidence, but the government has lined up all the Liberal members in this house to vote against such an increase, amounting to $25 per month.
I do not intend to name any members, although I could name one or two immediately, who today in their constituencies are endeavouring to lead their constituents to believe they are in favour of a straight increase. However vociferous they may be in and out of this house, and regardless of whether the government is right or wrong, Liberal members are always of the opinion that the government is always right.
Having said that, let me now refer to a matter of major importance. This legislation ought not to be passed until we have received an answer to the question regarding the position to be taken by the federal government when one province or another passes legislation giving that province the power and authority to grant old age pensions. It is not just a coincidence that this legislation was put of! for weeks and months, and suddenly rushed
December 15, 1966	COMMONS
Old Age Security Act Amendment into the house when the government of Quebec decided to claim jurisdiction in respect of old age pensions.
Mention has been made of the British North America Act and the section dealing particularly with old age pensions, namely Section 94A. I should like to read it again because it does not require any interpretation. Any layman or any individual who is able to read English or French can interpret this section and realize what it means. It reads:
It is hereby declared that the parliament of Canada may from time to time make laws in relation to old age pensions in Canada, but no law made by the parliament of Canada in relation to old age pensions shall affect the operation of any law present or future of a provincial legislature in relation to old age pensions.
In the month of April, 1963 the Prime Minister enunciated a principle, which I queried at the time and still do, which was disruptive of Canadian unity. That was the declaration of the concept of two Canada. Today that concept is being departed from, retreated from and abandoned by the government. The government showed by action that it does not believe in the concept of one Canada. This government stated in 1963, 1964 and 1965 throughout this country that we were going to build up a kind of dual nation-not a duality of citizenship based on the rights of French or English Canadians-but dividing Canada into two parts. The rights go back to 1775, 1791 and 1865 as amended since then.
With all the propaganda force at its command the government has today backed away from that concept. We do not hear anything more about co-operative federalism. That was a doctrine held up as one of the great concepts that this government had evolved. Co-operative federalism as a concept is as dead today as the dodo. This government was the creator of that concept, and the destroyer of it.
I am sure the minister has had this legislation ready for a long time, and I am sure it represents hours and days of work. We asked repeatedly for this type of legislation because we were willing to accept half a loaf on the basis that half is better than none. The government refused to bring it forward until the Johnson government of Quebec said it intended to bring in old age pension legislation, assuming jurisdiction in this regard in the province of Quebec.
The minister is able to recognize the government's promise during the last election campaign to increase old age pensions by $25 per month, and he is also able to forget about that promise after a period of 13 or 14 months.

The minister possesses political agility and astuteness.

speechtext:
The hon. member for Kootenay East is one who understands agility possibly better than any other member of this house.
I should like to ask the minister what the government intends to do regarding this legislation. Surely, the government does not intend to gloss over this matter and get the measure through simply by sitting silent and inert. We want to know what is going to happen and what the government intends to do.
As a result of the amendment to the British North America Act of 1951, the provinces joined together in accepting the principle that the federal government could bring in old age pensions, but that amendment did not provide for exclusiveness. The very wording of the section indicates that it was intended to maintain and preserve this exclusive right of the provinces to provide old age pensions.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
I will read this section again so that there will be no mistake:
-but no law made by the parliament ol Canada in relation to old age pensions shall affect the operation of any law present or future of a provincial legislature in relation to old age pensions.
When the legislature of Quebec passes the legislation which is embodied in the Speech from the Throne and determines, as evidence by the declaration which has already been made, to appropriate exclusively to the legislature of that Province jurisdiction over old age security in the province, what will be the attitude of the federal government? When Mr. Lesage was premier all he did was to ask, and generally he received what he asked for because the Federal government did not want to argue with a province which saw eye to eye with it in the legions of liberalism. However, suddenly this government has developed a new concept, and co-operative federalism has died an unnatural death. I am sure the minister will have gone into this matter most thoroughly and his advisers will have given the fullest consideration to the eventualities which will arise if the legislation is passed in Quebec.
Will the minister say to the province of Quebec that section 94A gives the federal government the right to pass the legislation on old age pensions? Section 94A gives us no exclusive right whatsoever; we only have a permissive one. If the province of Quebec

passes legislation to provide a pension of $100 a month, is it the intention of the government of Canada to bring about something like the monstrosity which it brought forward in connection with health insurance? In the case of health insurance, the government accepted the principle of the duality of insurance plans. Does the government of Canada intend to hand over to the province of Quebec-by way of advance or by whatever other method is followed, such as a subsidy-an amount that will be sufficient to cover the total expenditure to be made by that province on old age pensions? The government finds itself in a desperate position, and I can understand the minister's unaccustomed silence in this regard.
The government finds itself today in a frightful predicament on the question of university education which was mentioned by the hon. member for Prince Edward-Lennox. He asked what the government intends to do about McGill University, and the answer was that they would not get into that problem because it is within the jurisdiction of the province.
However, when we were in office we were able to bring about a formula whereby the province of Quebec-at the time when Colonel Sauve was premier of that province-accepted the $27 million which had been amassed for university education, under a formula which was acceptable to both sides. However, under that formula the money that was paid to the province of Quebec for education could only be paid to those institutions that qualified. In other words, they qualified on a per capita basis in accordance with the same requirements which obtained in other provinces.
When this government took office it decided, in its wholesale denunciation of all those principles that had been acceptable for years to embrace the idea of co-operative federalism, under which the amount advanced to any one province for educational purposes could be used in any other area. In other words, what was paid to a province for university grants could be used for other purposes. This money was simply placed in a consolidated fund, and the designation of this sum for any one purpose was made by the legislature of that province.
Now, the government is in a fine jam. I am interested to hear how they will get out of it. If the legislature of Quebec passes this legislation-and if I read Mr. Lesage's views correctly he is certainly not going to oppose the adoption of this legislation-then what will

Old Age Security Act Amendment the government of Canada do? They can say that this will come up later. We want to know now what they are going to do.
A moment ago when a question was raised in a general way and reference was made to a submission to the Supreme Court of Canada, the minister gave it his full attention but did not articulate any reply or make any suggestion regarding the attitude of the government. I would like to hear him now, as an authority on this subject. He must be an authority in view of the tremendous amount of expenditure that is now being made for social security, much of which is within the jurisdiction of the provinces. Naturally, he will be able to place before us clearly and succinctly answers to the following questions: first, has the government departed from the constitutional position that it adopted regarding the concept of co-operative federalism, which has now become unco-operative federalism?
Second, will the government push any province into the position of having to accept a measure that is unconstitutional? Far be it from this government or any government to do that, so the answer would be in the negative. Then, what will the government do? What does the government intend to do when the legislation is passed by the legislature of Quebec and receives royal assent? This is something that the people of Canada have the right to know. We have seen too much chiseling away at our constitutional rights in the last three and a half years not to demand now an accounting in the particular matter that is before the house. I await with anticipation and interest the explanation which the minister will make on behalf of the government of Canada. When the question was asked in 1964, as quoted earlier by the hon. member for Peace River, no answer was given. It might have been theoretical then, but today we are approaching the moment of truth. The legislature of Quebec intends to legislate exclusively on this question which is within its jurisdiction as set out in the constitutional amendment now embodied in section 94A. If the minister cannot answer this question himself but requires the assistance of the Minister of Justice or the Solicitor General, who today has become to all intents and purposes the real law officer of the crown, then I suggest that this section be allowed to stand. Otherwise, the minister should give the committee a full, complete, comprehensive and intelligible explanation of what this government is going to do. If the section stands, the government will be able to produce those in charge of the justice department and Canadians will learn
December 15, 1966

once and for all where we are tending under this government.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
For three years this government has followed one policy and is now running in the opposite direction. We want to know what this government intends to do in this connection; and we have a right to know before this bill is given passage by parliament.
I see the Postmaster General is in his seat. He is a man for whom I have always had a high respect, and I should like to hear from him in this regard. Is he going to depart from the constitution? I should also like to hear from the associate minister of defence on this question. I think they are the only two ministers from Quebec in the house, and I want them in on this poll. I want to hear what is their attitude, not what they are going to say on the hustings in the province of Quebec or elsewhere in Canada but what they are going to say in parliament.

subtopic: PROVISION OF GUARANTEED INCOME SUPPLEMENT AND DETERMINATION OF PENSIONERS' INCOMES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, surely the right hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) was right in raising the questions he has just raised with the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. MacEachen) with regard to the legality of Bill No. C-251. Will the amendment to the Old Age Security Act reduce in any way the vested rights of Canadian provinces, not only of Quebec, but of any province?
In fact, section 94A of the British North America Act says very clearly:
It is hereby declared that the parliament of Canada may from time to time make laws in relation to old age pensions in Canada, but no law made by the parliament of Canada in relation to old age pensions shall affect the operation of any law present or future of a provincial legislature in relation to old age pensions.
Mr. Chairman, the province of Quebec has stated very firmly and straightforwardly that it intends to recuperate all its rights relating to old age security. In my opinion, it is obvious, in the spirit and the letter of the British North America Act, that old age pensions are a matter for the provinces rather than for the Canadian government.
However, it must be recognized that the Canadian government, some thirty years ago, took the initiative of giving the Canadian people legislation providing for the first old age pensions, the first old age assistance legislation in Canada.

Old Age Security Act Amendment
At that time, all provinces were consulted and the provinces in general, except for the province of Quebec, which was then under a Liberal administration, agreed to let Ottawa take over legislation concerning old age security and allowances. Mr. Taschereau, the then Quebec premier said that old age pensions would amount to promoting laziness, that they would prevent children from helping their parents, in a word that children would become distorted sons or daughters, refusing to help the aged. One year later, old age pensions were accepted in the province of Quebec, as in all other Canadian provinces.
Of course, Mr. Chairman, you have to be fair with those who, at that time, were administering the country, at the federal level; as a matter of fact, they showed the way, so that the provinces might accept old age pensions. At the time nothing prevented the province of Quebec, like the others, from passing legislation to provide for the old age pensions; but, the initiative came from Ottawa and not the provinces. When we say today that Ottawa invades the rights of the provinces, when the provinces themselves were passive, paralysed or unwilling to act, I think that we have no right to blame the federal government for everything it has done in the field of old age security over the last 30 years.
Mr. Chairman, that does not stop us, however, from seeing the facts clearly as concerns Bill No. C-251 now under consideration, which provides for an increase of the pensions up to $30 a month, subject to investigations. Amendments to abolish such investigations, have been declared out of order or defeated, so that we shall have those investigations, with regard to any person who will receive any supplement to the existing pension. Even a pensioner over 70 years old, to be entitled to any old age security supplement, will have to submit to those investigations.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
And I think, Mr. Chairman, that investigators and investigations will cost the Canadian taxpayers more than if the supplement of $30 proposed in the bill were granted to all those 65 and over.
It will create a bureaucracy stronger than the present one; it will be necessary to open throughout Canada offices which will cost millions of dollars to decide who is entitled to that supplement and who is not. And everyone knows that those investigations lead to gross injustice. It is obvious today when
December 15, 1966

Old Age Security Act Amendment it comes to granting a pension to someone who is not 68 at the present time.
I think that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. MacEachen) should have inquired a little more about the cost of those investigations in Canada to find out who is entitled to a supplement and who is not. What will be required then, and who will decide if a supplement of $10 instead of $30, of $15 instead of $25 should be paid? The minister should have set up requirements, so that the members of parliament would at least know where they are going with that new bill.
I understand that the government's intention is to reach its goal, that is a minimum guaranteed income for every Canadian citizen. I do not think that the pensions will help it attain that goal, because even $100 a month is only $1,200 a year. Now, the minister is fully aware that nobody can live decently on $1,200 a year in Canada, in view of the present cost of living. It seems to me that is a well known fact.
Mr. Chairman, an interesting point was raised the other day by my colleague, the hon. member for Chapleau (Mr. Laprise). He referred to a state pensioner of 65, 67 or 68 years of age, whose wife would only be 54, 55 or 58. She is not entitled to a pension due to her age. I should like to know whether two persons living together can manage with $105 a month for both of them. So, why is it not specified in the bill that when a man is eligible for a pension, his wife is also entitled to one?
At present, mothers of 55, 57 and 58 years of age must work as charwomen, at night in most cases, because her husband and herself are unable to live on $105 a month and even less on $75, as at present.
Mr. Chairman, it seems to me that the Minister of National Health and Welfare should have urged his cabinet colleagues to be as generous for older Canadians as they are, for instance, with regard to national defence, trade and commerce, and foreign countries. I say again that we do not object to helping underdeveloped countries of the world, but let nobody tell me that our older people who get $75 or $80 a month are well off. Some people earn approximately the same amount in other countries where the cost of living is much lower than it is here. If some persons or families are reduced to poverty or destitution in several countries, we also have some in Canada. And the older persons in many cases fall in that group.

Now, Mr. Chairman, I understand that this bill is liable to be amended or improved any time when this or the following government will take that decision, but nevertheless, it is necessary to take into account the facts in our country which are evident to the world and show that we are one of the richest countries. If such is the case, we cannot deny Canadians, our older citizens who have devoted their life to their country, Canada, who have worked for its development and improvement, the strict right to a bare minimum, the right to have a decent standard of living in any province of our country, while respecting the wishes of each one of the provinces for, according to the British North America Act, each province has real and unquestionable priority rights in this field.
Even if Ottawa took the initiative 30 years ago, it must still respect the spirit and the letter of the Canadian constitution. It is not a question of amending the constitution, but only of respecting it, and from the moment it is respected, Ottawa will have done the provinces a service. We will even be able to say that Ottawa showed them the way 30 years ago and that, seeing that they have reached a certain maturity, we now come back to the spirit and the letter of the constitution and allow them to develop or pass legislation which they have the right to initiate in the best interest of both their population and the whole country.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the day before yesterday I mentioned the very problem brought up today by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) and the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin). I was asking the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. MacEachen) to tell us, if a province should claim exclusive jurisdiction over old age security, whether he would be prepared to recommend that the federal government grant the province fiscal compensation to finance and administer a provincial old age secrity fund.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
The minister, of course, reaffirmed what the Prime Minister stated this week to the house, namely that the federal government feels reassured with this bill as concerns the constitutionality of the legislation; in other words, the federal government is occupying this field and intends to stay there.
In today's context, that line of reasoning makes sense, of course, because as long as one, or all the provinces do not pass any old age
December 15, 19S6	COMMONS
security legislation, the federal government does not have to express its views on the matter.
However, since the Quebec government has announced in the speech from the throne that it is determined to pass legislation and to occupy the whole field of old age security,
I think the federal government is now placed before an accomplished fact. The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Mac-Eachen) and the cabinet should, so as to dispel any confusion that might exist in the minds of Quebec taxpayers, answer the questions we have asked, more particularly those put by the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Allard) and for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin), and put today by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker).
It is obvious, as the Leader of the Opposition pointed out this afternoon, that, should a province want to exercise its jurisdiction over old age security under section 94a, the federal government must withdraw from that field.
If we consider the spirit of the amendment passed in 1951, we find, especially on the part of Quebec representatives, a statement of principle to the effect that the province of Quebec, at that time, agreed to let the federal government exercise jurisdiction as regards old age security, but nevertheless kept the right to exercise its own jurisdiction in such a field when it deemed it advisable.
Now, the taxpayers of the province of Quebec are asking themselves the following questions: Should the provincial government set up its own old age security plan, will the federal government continue to exercise its own jurisdiction in the field of old age security along with the provincial government? Supposing the federal government refused to withdraw from this field, in order to administer this provincial old age security fund, will Quebec taxpayers be subjected to double taxation? Will the federal government act like in the case of joint plans? When I directed my question to the minister, I had joint schemes in mind, of course. We know that the federal government, in the case of provinces having withdrawn from some joint plans, under this system of co-operative federalism so often mentioned by the Prime Minister, decided to grant them fiscal compensation in return for the amounts they were not collecting under those joint programs.
This afternoon, the hon. member for Peace River asked the minister whether there would be any possibility of this constitutional issue,
Old Age Security Act Amendment which is obviously not difficult to understand, being referred to the Supreme Court by the cabinet, so that it would have guide lines as to its exclusive jurisdiction in this field.
I must point out to the hon. member for Peace River that the premier of the province of Quebec stated before the Quebec legislature that the province of Quebec would not recognize the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court jurisdiction in this matter and that a decision by that court on old age security would not be valid. And this brings me to say that as a matter of fact, in the province of Quebec, the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court would not be recognized by provincial authorities, nor by the majority of the people concerning this constitutional jurisdiction in any field whatsoever, as to whether it belongs to the province of Quebec or to the federal government.
I believe it would be useless for the cabinet to refer this question to the Supreme Court, since the present premier of Quebec and even Mr. Lesage when he was premier of the province have often questioned the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court and the validity of its decisions as regards the constitutional character of our legislation. I believe it is useless for the cabinet to ask for the opinion of the Supreme Court.
We ask the federal cabinet to reassure Quebec taxpayers and set their minds at ease, before this bill is passed, as to its eventual attitude concerning the old age security plan.
Will the central government persist in keeping this taxation field and will the taxpayers of the province of Quebec have to withstand double taxation, since they will be called upon to pay the costs of a provincial old age security plan?
Evidently, the federal government, according to the statements made by the Prime Minister and the Minister of National Health and Welfare, intends to keep this taxation field.
In the reply to the question I had asked the day before yesterday, the Minister of National Health and Welfare said that according to the law and the constitution, any province is free to establish its own old age security plan.
Of course, the minister thereby suggests that the province of Quebec can establish its old age security plan, but this does not mean that the federal government will withdraw from this field which it now occupies.
In my opinion, according to section 94A, if a province wishes to exercise its jurisdiction in the field of old age security, the
December 15, 1966

Old Age Security Act Amendment federal government has to get out. I believe that such is the spirit of the said section 94A.
I actually believe that it is not necessary for the cabinet to obtain an opinion from the Supreme Court in this matter. One has only to read carefully section 94A, as the hon. Leader of the Opposition said this afternoon, to be convinced that if a province wishes to exercise completely its jurisdiction in matters of old age security, it is fully entitled to do so. I think that the federal government should withdraw from a field that it occupies at present.
To my mind, there is only one solution the federal government should consider and I believe the hon. Minister of National Health and Welfare can give us an answer before this bill is passed. The federal government should say this to the provinces: If you decide to set up your own old age security plan and administer it yourself, the federal government is willing to deal with you in this regard, as it does in the case of joint programs.
I ask the minister earnestly to give us an answer. The matter is of the utmost importance and the present situation is unsettling for Quebeckers. It is only fair and sensible to give us a firm reply, positive and definite, concerning his jurisdiction with regard to old age security if Quebec should decide, as it has clearly indicated it will, to take over exclusive jurisdiction in that field.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)

Mr. Chairman, from what we heard since the beginning of the discussion on this bill, it is obvious that every objection seems to be of a constitutional nature. However, in spite of the numerous requests put to him in this regard, the Minister of National Health and Welfare refuses stubbornly to reply to the important and essential question that representatives of all parties, as well as the independent member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Allard) have been asking these last few days, namely: does section 94A of the British North America Act go against the bill now moved by the government in this house?
I think that the minister would help us enormously to shorten the debate and give it some direction if he had the courtesy to tell us clearly, without equivocation or shillyshallying, as the minister responsible for presenting that legislation to the house, how he defines the responsibility of the federal government with regard to the application of that legislation under section 94A. It is not necessary to be very acutely aware of constitutional matters, Mr. Chairman, to see in


black and white, at page 480 of Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, fourth edition, what is stipulated in section 94A. Here is part of it:
-but no law made by the Parliament of Canada . . . shall affect the operation of any law present or future-
It seems to me that the safeguard which the legislators included in the British North America Act is clear and protects the provincial legislatures against interference or centralization by the federal government.
Since I have other remarks to make, I am wondering if the minister is not being unfair and ill-disposed by refusing to take a stand and define the meaning he gives to that section 94A, since it is our only objection, but the main one, to that legislation.
I see that the minister is engrossed in the newspapers. Who knows but he may be reading precisely about objections raised in the house by hon. members who represent all the people of Canada. Personally, I represent a Quebec riding and I must therefore speak up for the interests of my province. Hon. members from other provinces have also made known their opposition to that legislation under that very same section 94A which is clear, unambiguous, and does not lend itself to any misunderstanding or even to a technical or legal interpretation.
In the meantime, Mr. Chairman, the minister is turning a deaf ear.
Why does he stubbornly refuse to make his position clear? What is the minister's interpretation of section 94A as far as it applies to old age pensions? The section is quite clear and it seems to me that the minister should give us an answer. If the minister says that his bill is not contrary to the B.N.A. Act, that it is not a challange to the Canadian constitution, in short, if he can give us the assurance that his bill is not contrary to the spirit behind all the legal opinions which contributed to bringing forward the 1951 amendment to the B.N.A. Act I say that he is wrong and that he is leading the country politically toward serious, to say the least, constitutional difficulties, as far as the future of this country is concerned.
If agreements between the central government and the provinces are not respected, Mr. Chairman, then what will be, in the future? Would the Minister of National Health and Welfare want, seriously and deliberately, to be instrumental in creating a strong disagreement between the provinces and the
December 15, 1966	COMMONS
central government? Is that the spirit of cooperative federalism we have heard so much about since his government took office? If the minister would only answer our questions instead of showing silent arrogance, indifference and irresponsibility toward parliament-an attitude which has become apparent over recent years-I think serious problems could be avoided, problems which could become more serious if the government does not, as it should, spell out its understanding of the country's constitutional problems.
Some members of the house have called for constitutional committees and advocated measures so that the central government and the provinces would cooperate more closely. The present government has always postponed the matter. It has studied, it will study again; it has considered and will reconsider those problems, but has never made a positive, firm, unequivocal decision on those fundamental problems concerning the compliance with the provisions of the B.N.A. Act, a pact which has allowed us to live in a rather relative but, nevertheless, positive harmony in our country. Relying on a majority vote and availing himself of a numerical superiority, since the government can probably expect the support of the New Democratic Party, the minister wants to run counter to the B.N.A. Act and to the spirit which inspired it.

Mr. Chairman, I am told that I ask too much but, out of the 40 odd Liberal members, I should be able to find at least one who would have the courage to ask the Minister of National Health and Welfare to give a clear explanation with respect to his interpretation of this particular section. And I wonder, Mr. Chairman, why it is that we must always come back on everything, implore, urge the minister to tell us what he thinks, how he interprets or what his definition is of a section of the constitutional act. Is this so very difficult for the minister?
This afternoon the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) stated that he considered the minister to be a brilliant man. I find the minister is brilliantly silent, because he knows that he is presently unable to give us his legal, historical and constitutional definition of section 94A. This is not difficult and it would be very clear. I wish to point out to the hon. minister that if he refuses to answer, he can expect that we will expose him-as we will have to-on the electoral platforms of the province of Quebec, along with those of his colleagues who refuse to give clear and plain explanations.
Mr. Chairman, our senior citizens are in urgent need. Several are in an extremely deplorable financial position. I represent a riding where the majority of voters are of the working class, and when they get to a certain age, these people can no longer earn a living with their trade, profession or occupation. Most of them are without any means of livelihood and they must receive government assistance. Whether this help comes from the provincial or the federal government does not matter, as long as somebody helps them.
Well, the Quebec government has shown its intention to assist them, to try and meet their needs, and that is why the federal government does not have to interfere in that
December 15, 1966

Old Age Security Act Amendment field. It no longer has a priority nor a constitutional right to occupy the old age pension field, as it is doing at the present time, or as it wants to do.
The hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette) said earlier that the federal government had taken the initiative to legislate as far as old age pensions are concerned; he was right. When the federal government did that, the provinces had shown no interest -because they did not have the means to finance such a legislation. But now the province of Quebec has shown its firm intention to legislate in that field, and if the minister keeps on refusing us a more precise definition of section 94A, I say that he runs counter to the law, he kills, right from the start, anything that we might contribute in future on the constitutional amendments, when we have developed a system for the revision of the confederation pact.
Mr. Chairman, I insist, as member of this house, and I ask and order the minister to give us an answer, or his interpretation of this section of the constitutional act referred to by several members of this house.
Why does the minister refuse stubbornly to give us an answer? Is he unable to do so? Is he short of legal advisers. Or is it because his colleagues from Quebec, on whom he based all his political propaganda during the last election, are unwilling to commit themselves with him in connection with that bill? The people have the right to know the reason for this silence which we disapprove, this silence which indicates to the people of this country the poor sense of responsibility shown by the minister in the House of Commons towards the representatives of the people. I do not understand why there is no standing order in this house compelling the minister to give explanations and state clearly his position about the discussion of a basic and unalterable principle, that is whether the minister is acting legally or illegally. I maintain, for my part, that he now acts illegally from a constitutional standpoint by forcing Quebeckers to submit to his act instead of the Quebec legislation as prescribed by the constitution.
Mr. Chairman, it is obvious that the members, and the minister knows it, are in a very difficult position or will be in a very difficult position when the time comes to vote for or against Bill C-251, because of the political aspect it implies. But we also know that the government is not honest in introducing this legislation. Knowing already that the provincial government intends to vindicate its constitutional rights in that field, the present government and the minister place the members in a situation which does not correspond to reality and which may be interpreted as a denial of the advantages which we want to provide to our senior citizens, if we vote against the bill. And if we vote for the bill, it means that we are accomplices of the minister in betraying the provisions of the British North America Act.
That, then, is the dilemma to which this bill and the minister's silence reduce us. If the minister gave us a clear definition, an accurate interpretation of the act, I believe we could far more honestly and objectively take a stand. I feel that the minister will be responsible for whatever treasonable acts are perpetrated by his own colleagues of the province of Quebec, when the vote is taken on this bill if he does not throw some light on his present stand.
We know, Mr. Chairman, that the N.D.P. members will vote for it blindly and without hesitation. Mr. Chairman, I have no intention of prolonging this debate. Last Tuesday, on second reading, that is before consideration in committee, I had the opportunity of making comments on the subject matter of the bill as well as on its constitutional implications.
I followed with a great deal of interest this afternoon the speeches of hon. members and particularly those of members of the official opposition. The one who has just resumed his seat, the hon. member for Sainte-Marie (Mr. Valade), as well as the speaker who preceded him, the hon. member for Charlevoix (Mr. Asselin), asked the minister some very judicious and important questions.
The hon. member for Sainte-Marie is wondering why the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. MacEachen), or the government, refuse to divulge their position and their opinion on the constitutional implications of this bill. Although the minister, it seems, does not want to answer, I think we were given a very solemn and imposing answer by another minister of the crown, the Associate Minister of National Defence (Mr. Cadieux) when we were examining another bill in this house during the present session. If I remember rightly, it was the bill concerning the creation of a cultural centre in Canada.
When some hon. members talked about the constitutional implications of this other bill, the Associate Minister of National Defence rose to condemn as shenanigans all these constitutional points often raised in this house by hon. members and based on the British North America Act. Yes, such is the attitude of Liberal members of this house and the cabinet ministers who come from the province of Quebec; for them, as for the government and the whole cabinet, constitutional
11171
Old Age Security Act Amendment implications are merely shenanigans. Hon. members should not expect an answer either for no government has ever shown such systematic obstinacy in not giving this house and the country explicit statements in order to eliminate undue conflicts. On the contrary, the government is aggravating those conflicts.'
As the hon. member for Charlevoix pointed out, the government of the province of Quebec, through its new premier, Mr. Daniel Johnson, has already stated publicly that it would not accept that this point be decided by or referred to the Supreme Court of Canada.
His predecessor, Mr. Lesage, also rejected the authority of the Supreme Court as far as mining rights on the continental shelf were concerned. In that matter, in that parallel responsibility as set out under section 94A, it is clearly stipulated that a jurisdiction, a prior and exclusive responsibility is granted to a province, when it decides to enter into that field of action.
The Supreme Court, with due respect to its honourable members, is not a body which can rule on constitutional opinions and conflicts between the central and provincial governments within the federative system in which we are living. In a federative system, the central government as well as the provincial governments are equal and autonomous in their respective responsibilities. A body appointed by one level of government is not apt to rule on conflicts which could occur between the central and provincial governments.
I know quite well that before 1941, we had an objective and constitutional authority, namely the privy council in London, as decided in 1867. Now, when the two parties concerned, either the central and provincial government or provincial governments, disagreed on the interpretation of the constitution, the privy council in London delivered its ruling on the appeal. Before 1949, there was an objective organization to settle the disputes between two levels of equal and autonomous governments within a federative system. But the federal government of the day abolished appeals to the privy council, which was a very good thing, not from the viewpoint of the constitution but of the emancipation of Canada, of the achievement of domestic and international sovereignty. Among the signs of sovereignty, an independent and selfgoverning country within the commonwealth

Old Age Security Act Amendment of nations had the power to decide its contentious matters, in last report, and it is under the provisions of the Statute of Westminster, of December 11, 1931, that the privy council, in London, was abolished as a final court of appeal in 1949. Since 1949, we do not have in our country an objective constitutional court, whose members would be appointed by the central and the provincial governments to represent precisely those various viewpoints, within federalism, of the various governments with regard to their equality and autonomy.
For the above reasons, the Quebec government and probably other provincial governments if they want to speak more openly, and millions of Canadians, are of the opinion that there is no court in our country to provide objective opinions on constitutional interpretations. And this government is always dragging its feet in this matter as well as in many others.

It is not the legislators of this parliament who have to And, in 1966, a solution to the problems of our time and the necessary constitutional reforms, consistent with normal changes occurring over a 100-year period. No. It is not the legislators of this parliament who have to determine and discuss those problems. This Liberal government has created an unofficial committee of public servants, who are giving advice to the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) or other members of the cabinet, in regard to possible reforms or adjustments. I think it is a serious mistake from the democratical as well as the legislative point of view.
How unfortunate that this should happen only a few weeks before we celebrate our centenary, since in a few weeks from now, it will be the beginning of the year 1967, meaning a record of 100 years for this magnificent country made up of so many Canadians of good faith from one ocean to another. Why is it that those Canadians do not understand each other sufficiently? Why is it that some, in a corner close to the Pacific ocean, and some others, close to the Atlantic ocean, are at times under the impression that they do not know each other and that it is very difficult to establish national understanding and brotherhood? I say that this Liberal government is greatly responsible for such

a situation, for it has refused, since January 18, since the opening of this session, to give the Canadian parliament, the members of which come from different sections of this country, the opportunity to openly discuss, specify, establish constitutional taxation reforms, through a joint committee of both houses. Personally, I may have particular reforms in mind and at heart, specific reforms that some Canadians will find drastic, but I am ready to discuss the matter. I want to exchange views in an official way, through a committee appointed to this effect. I am sure I will be able to make concessions, as other members who might sit on that committee so as to enable Canada precisely to turn toward a better, a much more efficient federation than the one we have known until now and the centenary of which we are going to celebrate.
I will always maintain that the present government, by refusing to set up this committee, makes no effort to establish, realize and materialize national harmony and brotherhood.
Mr. Chairman, how do you expect provincial representatives to get along with their federal counterparts with respect to every problem that comes up, when our parliament denies us the opportunity-as intelligent human beings-to define, organize, direct and activate the different levels of government for the next one hundred years.
Mr. Chairman, I hope the hon. Minister of National Health and Welfare will make his position known before the end of the debate. Let him not hesitate; we are prepared to hear him through, even though his views may be different from ours. But we want to hear what he has to say and let him not resort to this evasive way of going about things. The present government may very well decide unilaterally to embark upon a supplementary aspect of old age security, but it is not a Unitarian system of government we have in Canada.
We live in a federative system. There will be conflicts. The Quebec government said so clearly, and I am sure that the premiers of other provinces will do so shortly, and this will occur again.

Mr. Chairman, what worries me is that, if we delay passage of legislation which fulfil some needs, because there are terms we want to discuss here, it would be detrimental to the senior citizens who are anxious to receive those benefits; indeed, they are not much impressed by constitutional problems. Besides, what really counts for them is their cheque, and I wonder whether some compromise could not be found to settle the matter.
For instance, if any province should decide to pass legislation on old age pensions, I would think that the government should grant fiscal compensation to that province and transfer its responsibility to it. This would probably be a compromise that would make the government project more acceptable to those who now raise constitutional arguments against it.
Mr. Chairman, from my point of view, I cannot object to it because of a vital and urgent need for an increased old age pension to the senior citizens. This settles it. From there, let us strive to rejuvenate the constitution, straighten all those things, let lawyers agree among themselves-this may never be, perhaps it is wishful thinking-to try and arrive at an acceptable constitution formula.
A while ago, as I listened to my friends from Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Grafftey) and from Sainte-Marie (Mr. Valade) and even to my deskmate from Sherbrooke (Mr. Allard), who is a member of the legal profession and whose knowledge of constitutional matters I quite often admire, I said to myself:

I was thinking of my own province and I was asking myself: In my province, at least, are people in agreement on some formula? Do people know what they want actually? Now, I do not feel that we are in agreement, and I still have fresh in my memory this remark from a previous Quebec minister who, also, was quite convinced that the constitution had to be revamped as soon as possible but, as he said: "The time does not seem ripe, since we are not in accord yet."

I believe rather that we should choose in the ten provinces people of recognized qualifications and uprightness, people who are not influenced by partisan considerations, who, in their respective fields, are acknowledged as authorities, and then form what I have called already a sort of Council of Wisemen. These wisemen, sitting around a table, will establish the good will dialogue as suggested by the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi, and thereafter will offer to the responsible provincial authorities and the federal government an acceptable constitution formula.
But are we going to wait for that before we give our old people and our sick what they need? I do think so, Mr. Chairman. I am not so exacting, while not condemning those who are, honestly and sincerely, because I feel the need here is vital, fundamental, and that our old people need those things. Mr. Chairman, I listened with a good deal of interest to the speech of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) and to those of all the hon. members who represent the province of Quebec in this house.
At the present time, we are dealing with legislation which is of interest not only to the people of Quebec but also to every Canadian citizen. During the last election campaign, I remember, we promised $100 a month to each and everyone if our party came to power, and at that time, we could hear our opponents say: We shall give you $125 a month. But now that they are in the house, they sing a different tune. The party in office now introduces a piece of legislation and says: All those who received $75 at 70 years of age, without investigation, will now get $75 at 69, 68, 67 or 65 until everyone gets a pension at 65.
The position in which our fellow citizens find themselves in every province-and here I refer in particular to those in our own province-is that $75 a month is not enough to live decently.
When an additional amount of $30 is offered, but subject to a condition, in my opinion, it is a little undignified because the $30 difference is equivalent approximately to the increase in the cost of living, in Quebec as well as in the rest of Canada.
A little earlier, when we are dealing with the legal and constitutional aspect, it was stated that the province of Quebec had refused it. I think that it is the leader of the Quebec Creditistes who said: "It is Ottawa which took the initiative." I remember that, as if it were yesterday, because at that time I was entering provincial politics. It is true that the premier in office of that time refused, and he refused during seven years, to grant the old age pension to the people of our province, but was he wrong or right? That is a question one can rightly ask.

DEBATES	December 15, 1966
Mr. Chairman, at that time the province of Quebec had a yearly income of $75 million only, when today, its income reaches the $2 billion mark. As far as income is concerned, the province of Quebec at the present time is one of the richest in the Canadian confederation. But we fought, in 1936, claiming the old age pension for the people of Quebec because at that time, we were paying taxes to the federal government. Today, the problem is the following. The government wants to have investigations, to search through people's lives, to worry the aged, those who have $500 in the bank, the workers who managed to acquire a small property over 30 or 40 years and tell him: "Now you are going to assess your income to see whether you have a monthly income of $60 or an annual income of $720; if you do, you will lose your $30 completely.
People will be in a position where they are going to ask themselves: Are we going to make a false statement? Are we not going to take our $1,000 out of the bank and bury it?" Do they want all taxpayers in our province and in our country to act as hypocrites? I am reluctant to accept that, Mr. Chairman, and I think that the suggestion that was made, not only by our party but by almost every party and even by the Independents to give the full allowance to everybody, without asking any questions, would have solved the problem.
But the problem facing us at present is a constitutional one and as I have spent 19 years in Quebec, I have become sensitized to that question. Respect for laws in the provinces is very important to me. I know the federal government has rights, and that it is the responsibility of federal members to preserve them. But members in Ottawa also represent one province or another, and in our case, we represent the province of Quebec. With a population of 6 million out of the 20 million people in Canada, I feel we are representing quite an important area.
Clause 92A is probably the clearest of all clauses in the British North America Act. As regards clauses 91 and 92, there are discussions. It is being said "they are subjects of exclusive provincial legislation", but in a further clause, one can read:
-nevertheless, In case of urgency, In case of warhot war or cold war-
-the federal government may be granted the right that we regarded as exclusive to the provinces.
December 15, 1986	COMMONS
But in clause 94A, there is no doubt, whether it be past, present or future, a province may at a given moment, claim the exclusive right in this matter. Even if the federal government lays claim to that right, I am not denying it such a right, I say that if the province claims it, I wonder why the minister and the government persist in provoking the provinces.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
In Canada, as we know, we are going through a difficult period at this time. We are going through a troubled period. And in the province of Quebec-more than anywhere else perhaps-people are awakening and claiming their rights. And that is the reason why I was listening with pleasure to the leader of the Conservative party (Mr. Dief-enbaker) when he said, a while ago, that he wanted constitutional rights to be observed. And I heard other members saying: "We dread the decisions of the Supreme Court". Thus spoke the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Allard) and other members.
And the present premier of Quebec, as well as his predecessor, Mr. Lesage, are unanimous in saying that they do not accept, in certain cases, decisions from the supreme court regarding constitutional matters. This is no wonder. The court in question is organized and appointed by the federal government; consequently, it cannot be a good judge in such a delicate and important field.
Concerning the arguments put forward as to whether the federal government should readily grant the provinces what they are asking for, Quebec demands recognition of a right to which it is entitled under the constitution. There is no doubt about that. But instead of saying yes, the federal government is defying Quebec once again. This situation occurred often enough. In my opinion, the time has come for the present cabinet, for the minister there-who means well, I admit it -to take a position which would contribute to better relations between the federal and the provinces. Actually, it would be very simple if the minister would only say: we will give the fiscal compensation to the provinces requesting it, because they are entitled to it. This, I think, is the viewpoint of my party: provinces should be given fiscal compensation; discussions with our provinces at every turn should come to an end.
As a matter of fact, the federal government will spend large amounts to initiate inquiries. It would be so simple if it only said to the provinces: administer the plan, whether it is $75, $100, $105 or $125 a month;
Old Age Security Act Amendment the province may provide whatever payment it wants, and the federal government will grant it fiscal compensation, guaranteed by its own legislation, as it is bound to give it to all other provinces who will not accept to administer themselves the scheme under consideration in the house.
I am surprised to note that the ministers from Quebec do not stand up here to demand the rights of their province. I am surprised to note that members who, during election campaigns, in the province of Quebec, for all sorts of reasons, contend that their party is the defender of the rights of minorities, of provincial rights, do not stand up now to demand those rights here. They know that all parties in the Quebec legislature are unanimous in claiming those rights. But here, what the official opposition, the Creditistes, the independents ask for is not heard. One would say that their arguments fall on deaf ears. The minister does not want to; his attitude is such that it is provoking a reaction in the province at a time when the latter must remain calm, when it must sense what is coming, when it must prepare the future. The government in power has only about 50 members in whom the Quebec people have placed their confidence. Those men have no right today to cast a vote which would prevent the province of Quebec from getting what belongs to it, from claiming, in all fairness, the right to admister and to apply within Quebec, for Quebec and by Quebec, the social legislation which comes under its jurisdiction.
I think the minister would do well to review his legislation and to bring forward some amendments that are imperative. I am convinced, Mr. Chairman, that we could then bring back a climate of peace and good will between federal and provincial governments.
But especially, I would like a climate of good understanding between my province, the province of Quebec, and the government of my country.
