speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I must express my appreciation to the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Finance for recognizing that this bill, relating to the League Savings and Mortgage Company, involves the incorporation of a company which operates in competition with the operations of a credit union incorporated under the Loan Companies Act. This bill was considered by the committee on finance, trade and economic affairs, but it will be perhaps February or March before we will have the proceedings of that committee printed.
Perhaps I should repeat what I said at the second reading stage of this bill. For many years I have been a member of a credit union and I thoroughly endorse the principles behind the functions of such an organization. I do so because this is one method by which people can control their own financial investments. One principle in respect of credit unions is that a member has one vote regardless of the number of shares he may own. An individual member has only one vote regardless of whether he owns ten times as many shares as another member. This is in direct conflict to the principle which has been accepted by companies incorporated under the Loan Companies Act. To put it clearly, if an individual owns 100 shares in the League Savings and Mortgage Company he would have 100 votes whereas an individual who owns a thousand shares in a credit union would have only one vote, not 1,000 votes. There is this important difference between these two types of organization.
I hope this conflict will be cleared up by the sponsor of this bill before we complete this stage of our consideration. That hon. member did a very good job of explaining the purposes of this bill at the time he introduced it. He outlined the background of this proposed corporation. Inasmuch as the League Savings and Mortgage Company has been founded by a credit union movement in Nova Scotia, and inasmuch as it is in essence an extension of a
23033-708J
Private Bills
credit union's financial operations, owned, directed and controlled by members of a credit union, hon. members of this committee are well advised to take some step to ensure that this company will be of benefit to the credit union movement. Any step which can be taken by this parliament to strengthen the credit union movement is a worthwhile step.
There is a very serious conflict between the philosophies of the credit union movement and companies operated on the basis of individual control.
[DOT] (6:10 p.m.)
The credit union movement has apparently found this to be the only mechanism they can use to reach the end which they desire. This is an effort to put together two philosophies which run counter to each other. On the one hand, we are seeking to give effect to the desire of the credit union movement to enlarge its activities into the savings and mortgage field, and on the other we desire to give effect to the principle of ownership and control which is contained within the credit union movement. However, we are doing this by superimposing another requirement, that of financially based ownership. With all due respect to the hon. member who is sponsoring the bill and with sympathy and understanding for the credit union movement, I submit that the committee should not be content simply to pass the bill because it seems to be a good idea. We should take a look into the future and plan some steps to guarantee and protect the rights of the credit union people by ensuring that the League Savings and Mortgage Company shall always act in accordance with the credit union philosophy and principles.
Of course we would be much better off in this regard if we had on the statute books some credit union legislation under which groups such as this one could operate. We should have a federal credit union law which would assist credit unions in joining their resources together so as to expand beyond the bounds of the individual credit union and encompass other fields of financing, which is not now possible with the limited resources which a small, community based, credit union might have.
Over the years it has been the hope of many of us that the parliament of Canada some day would get around to drafting legislation in the credit union field. If we had such legislation it would then be possible for the League Savings and Mortgage Company to apply for incorporation in this fashion and to apply for the expansion of the credit union movement for

the purposes desired by this particular company. I should like to make reference to clause 7 of the bill even though we have not yet reached that clause. The powers and limitations of the incorporating act of the League Savings and Mortgage Company would then read as follows:
The company has all the powers, privileges and immunities conferred by, and is subject to all the limitations, liabilities and provisions of the credit unions act of Canada.
This would be a far more desirable way of approaching this matter. To my knowledge, this is the first time that a group of credit unions has desired to embark on this type of project, and I hope it will not be the last time.
I hope that other credit unions, even in the absence of a beneficial credit union law relating to them, will see the advantages which might come from this sort of incorporation. I hope that the government will recognize that something has been taking place in the credit union movement to which it should have given some thought several years ago.
I hope the government will take the course of drafting a federal credit unions act to enable credit unions all across the nation to expand rightfully and correctly into the fields of mortgage lending for housing developments, for individual home ownership, for investment for the expansion of credit union plans, and for the expansion of loans to co-operatives. The co-operatives have a comparable philosophy, except that they deal in the field of production and distribution rather than in financing.
I would strongly urge the government to appoint one of its ministers who may not have much to do-and there are many like that-to oversee the question of federal credit union legislation. He could, in consultation with the credit union movement, start drafting a federal credit unions act so that we might have in the near future some guiding legislation of which this parliament would approve for the advancement of the philosophy according to which human beings who own, control and direct their own means of production, distribution and, in this instance, financing, are far better off.
In the past the parliament of Canada has never hesitated to come to the aid of the free enterprise section of the economy by means of protective legislation. The company now under consideration is being incorporated under the Loan Companies Act, a law which was conceived by the government and passed by parliament. It is designed to enhance the position of the free enterprise section of the economy in the field of loans. We have the

Companies Act, the Small Loans Act and a variety of other public laws which are designed to increase the position of the money interests. I submit that the time is overdue for the enactment of legislation which would enhance the position of the individual in the society.
A door is being opened to us and a group of credit unions is coming to parliament and saying: "Let us incorporate in this way because it is the only way in which we can do it. In this way we are giving to you an indication that federal legislation is lacking in the field of credit unions". I hope that the government will take cognizance of that fact, and take a serious look at it.
I take note of the fact that only one minister of the crown is present in the house this evening, namely the associate minister of defence. I notice that he is listening attentively, and I hope with approval, to what I am saying. I do not know the extent of his duties in the department of defence, or what his position will be when the forces are unified. Knowing his sympathies for the rights of the individual and his desire to preserve those fundamental rights and freedoms, and particularly knowing there is perhaps a stronger belief in those rights in his province than in other parts of Canada, I am sure that he will immediately see the advantage that will accrue to human beings if this government enacts laws to protect the rights of the individual in the financial world. Mr. Chairman, the last words uttered by the sponsor of the bill add some weight to the remarks made earlier by the hon. member for Skeena about the need for what I would term a federal co-operative charter for Canada, of which appropriate credit union legislation would be an important segment.
[DOT] (6:30 p.m.)
If my recollection is correct, years ago in this country in the insurance field there were organized what at the time were called mutual insurance companies. According to my information they were orginally organized in rural areas of Ontario. They were closely related to what today are known as co-operatives, or credit unions. They were set up under legislation with the idea that their policyholders would be shareholders. They were to be organizations democratically run, comparable and similar to credit unions being operated in the various provinces of Canada that already had credit unions.
Over a period of time, because of the legislation they were incoporated under, the effective control of these organizations passed out of the hands of the original organizers. The companies became companies controlled by minority blocks of shareholders, that is in numbers of people controlling the companies. Many of the older insurance companies, some of them still operating in Canada today and carrying the mutual label, have long since ceased to come within the real meaning of thcit term.
I share the concern of the hon. member for Skeena that this should not happen to organizations such as this, because this body is obviously being put forward as a bona fide body by the credit union movement of Nova Scotia. I am sorry that we have not the full printed proceedings of the committee before us when we are considering this bill, but I thank the hon. member for Pictou for having given a summary of the representations made to the committee by the credit union people from Nova Scotia. I thank him for the information he gave of the background of this bill at the second reading stage.
This bill, I believe, is another example of the sort of limitation placed on the growth of organizations like credit unions because of the lack of appropriate legislation. We take great pride in this country in our democratic

process, that every citizen of the country considered adult and in his right mind, who has not been incarcerated for a criminal offence, has the right of the franchise. We make a great deal of one vote for every citizen, and that in our election process all citizens are equal in determining what eventually takes place in our representative institutions of parliament and the legislatures of the country. In spite of our pride in this political democracy, we effectively deny to the people who want to build an economic democracy the necessary machinery by which they can do this. In my view the terms of this bill show how difficult it is for people like the credit unionists of Nova Scotia to set up this kind of financial institution in a way that will make it clear to all the world that it is what it is. I am sure the credit unionists of Nova Scotia are proud they are taking this step. I am sure they have not changed much from what they were a few years ago, when I had the opportunity as a member of a committee to listen to a presentation on another matter by a credit union spokesman from that province.
At a cursory glance this bill seems no different from 101 other bills incorporating mortgage or finance companies across this country. This appears to be an ordinary company governed by the same principles, as the hon. member for Skeena says, that govern people in other companies wielding a big economic stick. It is unfortunate that this kind of mechanism has to be used for such an organization to be incorporated. Members of parliament ought to do something about this. A few years ago, in another field of the co-operative movement in Canada, the desires of co-operaters to develop insurance institutions in accordance with the principles of economic democracy were denied because of the lack of appropriate general federal legislation. It was impossible for them, within the framework of existing federal law, to ensure that economic democracy would prevail through the normal democratic principle of delegated representation at annual meetings.
I am happy to see this bill coming forward. I participated in the credit union in my home town. I saw that credit union grow from a small organization to one which now has several branches owning two or three nice buildings. It has a full time staff and is a successful business enterprise. It still retains the principles of economic democracy in its functioning. The credit union movement in my province has become an important factor, as a financial institution, within the province. That is true of individual credit unions and of the credit unions collectively, coming under such bodies
December 15, 1966

as the credit union league and the central credit union of the province.
For a long time the credit union movement in British Columbia operated with inadequate provincial legislation. The attempts made- and this, I suggest, will happen in Nova Scotia-to provide services that people needed where there was a need for lending funds, were hampered by lack of provincial legislation to make this possible.
I am happy to say forward steps have been taken in recognizing the growing place of credit unions. Those steps have been taken within the framework of provincial legislation, and our central credit union now operates, as I understand it, within reasonably satisfactory provincial legislation. I assume the same process is taking place within provincial fields of legislation in some of the other provinces of Canada.
[DOT] (6:40 p.m.)
I had an interesting discussion with a person from the province of Quebec who is associated with the provincial department of co-operatives. He told me something of his work in helping to expand and make more attractive the operations of the credit union movement within that province. We in this parliament can no longer afford to ignore the credit unions and the co-operatives of Canada. As far as the parliament of Canada is concerned, such organizations do not even exist. Those of the type before us now demonstrate that quite well.
I support the passing of this bill with some reluctance. I do so because this appears to be the only legislative mechanism which is open to us at the present time. And I do so with some regret, because this is an important area of the activities of this parliament which has been ignored for too long. Ever since I became a member of the house, this question has been regarded as one which must eventually be dealt with. Yet no effective proposal has come forward from the treasury benches. It is time some concrete proposal was placed before parliament for consideration.
The mere fact that this bill is before us in its present form is, to me, sufficient demonstration of the great gap in our concept of what is required. There are acts galore having to do with the incorporation of private companies of one kind or another. It is about time that we who like to boast about political democracy took steps to make it possible for those Canadians who want economic democracy to develop more easily the institutions in which they believe and which would be of advantage to them.

Mr. Chairman, this afternoon we heard members of this house ask the minister to state his position with regard to section 94A of the B.N.A. Act.
Far be it from me and previous speakers also, I think, to take up the time of the house only for the sake of it. The meaning of section 94A is of vital importance and it is extremely important that the position of the minister and, therefore, of the government, should be clearly defined.
As I said earlier, we are not seeking to prevent the passage of Bill No. C-251, but it is clearly the duty of members of the house to ask the minister to clearly state his position.
December 15, 1966

As Quebec members, I feel it is in our interest to know the minister's intentions. If we insist, it is because the interpretation given to section 94A could give rise to some disagreement, misunderstanding or even legal disputes prejudicial to mutual understanding and unity in the country. That is why, when I spoke on Tuesday, December 13, as reported on page 11061 of Hansard, I asked the minister as plainly as possible how he understood section 94A or what position he intended to take in that connection. After quoting section 94A, I put a few questions to the minister that I should like to repeat now. I said, among other things:
It is impossible to ignore the wishes of any Canadian province-
Mr. Chairman, as you know the government of the province of Quebec, through its premier, Hon. Daniel Johnson, has expressed its intention of invading the field of old age pension. Section 94A gives him that right and when we ask the minister to establish his position, we merely wish to prevent any difficulty.
Later on I said:
I therefore ask him not to miss the opportunity to make his positions known, because if this is not done, there may be . . . between the two levels of government a misunderstanding.
I repeat this same warning today and I add, Mr. Chairman, that I can hardly understand and interpret the attitude of the Liberal members of the province of Quebec. Throughout the speeches made on this side of the house this afternoon, the members on the other side of the house gave us the impression that they were losing patience and that they were feeling ill at ease about our remarks. And we repeat over again for the hon. member for Saint-Henri, that we do not intend to resort to a filibuster or make trouble for the government, we merely wish to establish clearly our respective positions. This is our only intention.
[DOT] (7:10 p.m.)
And from my seat in the house, I had the opportunity to notice this afternoon a conversation going on between the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Mac-Eachen) and the Associate Minister of National Defence (Mr. Cadieux) which lasted a good while during the speech of one of my colleagues. I thought that the Associate Minister of National Defence seemed worried.
Mr. Chairman, the continual refusal and obstination of the hon. Minister of National Health and Welfare with regard to establishing his position certainly puts the Liberal
[Mr. Ricard.l
members from the province of Quebec in a difficult situation. They cannot but realize that one day they will have to account for their vote on this question. They will not be able to step back every time or to justify their position, as they did for example at the time of their vote on the second flag and when they voted in favour of nuclear weapons. The people of the province of Quebec will not stand for the Liberal members from their province refusing much longer to assume their responsibilities here in the House of Commons.
This is why I should like the minister- and that is all I ask of him-to answer our questions and let the hon. premier of the province of Quebec know what his position will be with regard to section 94A of the British North America Act.
The statement of the hon. premier of the province of Quebec was quite clear. He said that nothing would stop him, which means that he could even resort to double taxation. I do not think double taxation would be in the public interest. If the hon. minister will not state his position clearly, I would like my Liberal colleagues from the province of Quebec to let us know at least what will be their attitude and their reaction with regard to double taxation. One must remember, Mr. Chairman, that the premier of the province of Quebec has the support of the liberal opposition in Quebec. The leader of the opposition himself, Mr. Jean Lesage, said he was supporting the principle set forth by the premier of the province of Quebec. In this matter, he was supported by the former minister of municipal affairs (Mr. Laporte) and he even has in this house a member supporting him, namely the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Choquette) who has also declared himself in favour of the principle under which old age pensions should be administered by the government of the province of Quebec. speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, after listening to all the speeches this afternoon and on looking at this bill I am concerned about the legislative jungle into which we may be getting. I think there are a few principles which we have not yet considered. It has been stressed before that approximately 7 per cent of our population consists of people 65 years of age and over. In another 10 years this figure may go up to 10 per cent and it is quite possible that the rate of increase will rise more rapidly. I should like to make a point regarding taxation. If a tenth of our population becomes unproductive at the age of 65 they will increase the ranks of the unemployed but will still be consumers. This will put a big load on the younger generation, the wage earners of this country, and will create an imbalance in our economy. I think that in the future the trend should be to encourage these people to work beyond the age of 65 and to continue their productive years. I do not see why there should be an arbitrary age of 65
December 15, 1966

at which they should stop working. Some years ago the idea was prevalent that because of biological aging it was necessary to set a limit at which a person should stop working. Let us face facts. In 1900 the average age span of a person was 40 years but today, in 1966, the span of life extends to 70 years.
I submit that this fact should be seriously considered. The government says that it is short of money. I do not exactly agree with this but if it is so I think it is largely due to bad housekeeping. However, I will not go into that topic at the present time. The fact of the matter is that we have a growing aged population. Half the population of Canada is 25 years of age or under and in a decade the dividing line may be at the age of 35. There is no reason to doubt that as medical science progresses people could live to be 100. As a matter of fact, there is one place in the U.S.S.R. where research work is being done in the field of longevity. Their research has shown that people live to the age of 100 and are still able to continue productive work and to all intents and purposes are perfectly healthy. I do not know whether this fact has been authenticated but according to the reports of these scientists some people in that area live to the age of 125. This is a matter the house must consider because we are getting into a legislative jungle as far as the provinces are concerned. This is why, as the minister said, it would have been so much simpler to give the pensioners $100 a month across the board. Why didn't he?
[DOT] (7:30 p.m.)
As I have said before, we have an aging population and in this regard I should like to give an illustration of the economics involved to the committee. A friend of mine who had earned good money all his life retired on a pension of a little better than $15,000 a year. He had to quit work because of an arbitrary rule of retirement at 65. He laid around for a few months, visited here and there and finally got tired and accepted another post at $25,000 a year. Three years ago he was still holding down that position. He is paying tax on $40,000 in the United States where he lives. Why in the world tax a similar case in Canada on $25 a month? This is the point I am trying to make.
Let me look at the other side of the coin. What happens to people when they are prevented from working? If we look at the statistics and believe the medical scientists, geriatric societies and schools of medicine, people deteriorate when they stop working. It not
Old Age Security Act Amendment only shortens their lives but can make them bed patients or put them into a home. This is something all of are concerned about because very soon we too will be old. So this legislation is of great concern to us now and to the people who will follow us.
Compulsory retirement at age 65 solves nothing; it just creates problems. As the population increases productivity must increase because the people must be fed and looked after. This puts us on the horns of a dilemma. People who are taken out of production are still consumers so this puts a greater burden on the workers. I suggest that the financial burden placed on the people of carrying an increasing number of older citizens would be intolerable, with the life span increasing as it is today, if everyone stopped working at age 65. Therefore it follows that we must utilize to the utmost the productive efforts of our older people.
I have an interesting article before me which states that some companies and many individuals know that compulsory retirement is often the wrong answer to just one of the challenges which are presented to business. A compulsory retirement plan allows a company tactfully to unload those it no longer needs but it also prevents companies retaining people they want to keep. The article asks whether the Canadian National Railways, for example, really wanted to lose Donald Gordon. Donald Gordon could hold his place with anyone on the board but, though able, he had to retire. I have indicated how this sort of thing affects the economy. I suggest any principle which taxes elderly people who are working on an extra $25 a month is wrong.
Let me now come to the little people who belong to the labouring class, the sort of people who do not work for corporations, people who are now 65 or over. I am referring to the k!nd of people who have not worked in factories or in other organizations from which they receive a pension. They have never earned a lot of money. They have little or no income. There are about 150,000 of these people across Canada. Approximately another 475,000 have incomes of $1,000 or less. These are the marginal workers who have to do gardening or caretaking, and the ladies do babysitting. These are jobs they badly need.
Let me illustrate my point with an actual case. I know a man who is a gardener. He cuts the lawns of a property owned by a busy executive and looks after the flowers. He earns around $700 a year. He is a nice man who never had much education; I do not think
December 15, 1965

Old Age Security Act Amendment he got beyond second grade. But he does do a good job. He has an old car that he drives to and from his work. In the fall he covers up the plants and fixes everything up for the winter. As soon as spring comes and the ground is ready he tends the gardens and lawns for the rest of the season. He requires overalls, heavy boots and work shirts as well as a few tools.
Another case in point is that of a lady who babysits for three families when required. She does a little sewing. She really does not know what she earns but thinks it is somewhere in the neighbourhood of $600 to $800. She has never kept any books. She requires a few extra clothes, coats and overshoes for her work.
Both of these people are in the marginal labouring class and have had little education but are people to whom we owe a great deal. Many were born before 1900. What will these people be forced into if the minister's guaranteed income plan is put into effect? They are going to sit on the porch in the summer and deteriorate, and they will watch television in the winter. The man will do no gardening, and there are not too many others to replace him. Financially these two people will lose $25 to $30 a month by not working, but the man would have to spend more than this on his car, his clothes and his tools. Therefore he cannot afford to work. This man will be faced with deterioration, probably mentally as well as physically, and I do not think this is right. His incentive will have gone.
[DOT] (7:40 p.m.)
But this is not all, Mr. Chairman. Instead of encouraging him the government is discouraging him. It will destroy him. Idleness and boredom will lead to illness and soon he will go either to a nursing home or to a hospital. He will degenerate physically and mentally, and the government will have created but one more problem. It will have taken people out of their homes where they were self-sustaining and sent them to a nursing home or to a hospital much sooner than should have been the case. This is the situation that the government is creating. By so doing you remove the productivity of these men and women from the economy. And add to the burden of taxation on the younger people of the country. Make no mistake about that.
The younger people will have to support the institutions and hospitals populated by people who, but for the government's action, might


not have been there. People in such institutions will cost millions of dollars in lost productivity and for the care which will have to be given them in these institutions. The aged population must be kept working in the factories and in the fields. In the factories it is mandatory that workers retire at 65. Education and retraining-I know the minister has advanced views on this subject-are needed. We do not need a means test on our senior citizens but we do need education and retraining for our people. That is the course to be followed.
We ought to draw on the skills and experience of our old people. You can be as educated as you like but you only get experience through time, and that is what the government is forgetting in this bill. The older citizens should be kept working. They will be healthier and better adjusted for it and they will be producers as well as consumers. I am disturbed about this bill. I cited some cases to prove my point. Perhaps 100,000 people in Canada are similarly situated, for all I know. The minister does not know about this either. I have spoken of two people I know in one little town. What about similar people in other hon. members' constituencies?
I am disturbed about another thing. What will become of the medical care cards which people will have in the province of Ontario? The minister has taken away one month's salary from these aged people. He has taken away one month through this so-called gift of a guaranteed income of $30 per month. What will happen, Mr. Chairman? Those people will come under the $600 taxable income provision, and that means that they will pay $30 a year for their medical cards. I will not go any farther, but I could have mentioned many other things that are not right about this bill.
In fairness to those people who themselves cannot do anything about the matter, to the marginal workers and those people over 65 in good health who still want to work, who still want to perform a useful service, who still want to add to the productivity of the country, I shall move this amendment to proposed section 8, subsection 1 in clause 3:
That subsection (1) of new section 8 of clause 3 be amended by the addition of the following proviso thereto:
"Provided that no deduction shall be made In the case of a single person having earned less than three hundred and sixty dollars in the preceding year and in the case of a married person, otherwise qualified, having earned less than seven hundred and twenty dollars in the preceding years."
December 15, 1966

Mr. Chairman, we have witnessed today a small marathon in which the handful of French speaking Conservative members who managed to get elected in the province of Quebec vied with each other in trying to amend the Old Age Security Act.
They did not speak about the benefits to be derived from the amendment to this act nor, as did other hon. members of the opposition, about the social philosophy embodied in the bill. They did not, of course, speak about the welfare which will benefit a large part of the needy in the province of Quebec. They neglected the whole social aspect, the whole welfare side of the bill and chose to deal instead with the constitutional aspect.
And it is surprising to see this sudden start on the part of the French speaking Conservative members with respect to the constitution, they who have remained silent I do not know how many times when intrusion by the Conservative government of the time, in fields of provincial jurisdiction, was criticized. This sudden awakening occurs on more than just shifting grounds. In fact, three lines of the speech from the throne delivered in a legislative assembly have caused this sudden awakening. And yet, these three lines are far from a bill. Because of three lines which the government of the province of Quebec inserted in its speech from the throne, at the opening of the session, we suddenly discover this great flurry on the part of the Conservative members who cry out: "Watch out for the constitution," having no knowledge of the implications of those three lines for the future.
[DOT] (7:50 p.m.)
And it is that much more surprising to discover this happening immediately after a
Old Age Security Act Amendment federal-provincial conference, where all questions were discussed, and during which the government of the province of Quebec never once mentioned that they intended to take over old age pension responsibilities. This unilateral gesture on the part of the provincial government, coming immediately after a federal-provincial conference, is strange. And it is also strange to note that this unilateral action is being taken in a recognized field, within a field of joint jurisdiction and no one here can claim anything to the contrary.
Of course, the priority of jurisdiction can be discussed-and I would not like to discuss it here-but when a joint field of jurisdiction is chosen and a unilateral stand taken after a federal-provincial conference, it appears more clearly that the government of the province of Quebec is bent on picking a quarrel with the federal government and its quarrel rests on very shaky grounds.
It is strange also to see that suddenly a pact, an alliance is struck between the federal Conservative members of the province of Quebec and those of the Union Nationale. That pact is still fragile in view of the remarks made by the premier of Quebec who said that he had no alliance with the Conservatives of the province of Quebec. Therefore, the Conservatives of the province of Quebec are on their knees today before a provincial government which has given only three lines to that matter in the speech from the throne and on their knees before a provincial government which has clearly signified to the Conservative party that it did not want to co-operate with it.

And why do those same Conservative members, in another field oi joint jurisdiction, not ask their so-called Quebec friends, to busy themselves with research, which is of prime importance if we want to stand our ground in the world instead of dealing haphazardly with the well-being of our people?
Today, research is essential. But we have never heard of a Conservative member for the province of Quebec asking his Quebec friends to deal with it. There are three fields of joint jurisdiction where the Quebec government could work. But let the federal government introduce a bill that can be of benefit to the people of Quebec that can increase the well-being of people whose rights are denied, who are in need, and they rear up, take up the torch and want us to retreat before three words, three lines in the speech from the throne. What a queer bunch of members we have here before us, Mr. Chairman, to fight for the rights of the people of Quebec.
Would those members want us to give up our jurisdiction overnight so that old age pensions might be reduced in Quebec?
Are members not seeking to stir up those who voted for the Union Nationale in Quebec, and this seems to be the case when one witnesses what seems to be a putsch?
Mr. Chairman, what is important to consider at this time concerning old age security is the commitments of the government during this one session. That is what is important, and our friends in the N.D.P. should listen to this, as they have always preached that the social problems should be examined and solved as a total concept and not only within the framework of a matter of social security.
The federal government has announced a social assistance plan which will cost millions. It has had medicare passed, which will cost millions. It has announced a retraining program which will cost millions. All that in one session only. And today, the same government presents an amendment to the old age security act for a $30 increase for those in need.
Those are coherent social policies. But, Mr. Chairman, nobody at this stage can tell the total cost of all those commitments. Only time will tell us how many hundreds of millions of dollars we will have to spend to meet our commitments. In the field of retraining, we will have to train a large number of people because we must make up for time lost. And even more in the field of old age security since under the proposed legislation,

those who will qualify for a pension will be able to receive it at 68, 67, 66 and 65 years of age.
Hence, we have very important commitments now and for the future. I do not deplore that, but the stubbornness with which we persist trying to concentrate everything on a single social measure, when all the social field must be provided for, especially family allowances which have not been reviewed for a long time.
From 1957 to 1966, total expenditures for old age pensions went up from $473 million to $927 million, while for the same period, total expenditures for family allowances increased from $437 million to $551 million. It means that over a ten year period, the total amount for old age pensions increased by $450 million while the total amount for family allowances went up by $114 million only. If we consider that the legislation announced will entail foreseeable expenses of $280 million for the first year, and $40 million per year for the next three years, we can see that we will soon reach, that is in three years, an increase in 10 years of $1 billion for old age pensions whereas, to date there has been only an increase of $114 million in family allowance expenditure.
If our friends of the opposition would like to be reasonable in the case of old age pensions, they should ask the federal government to review family allowances as soon as possible. That is where we should strike and demand because even though we should keep our senior citizens in mind, we should also consider those who are preparing to become the working group of our population. And today, we notice that we have neglected for too long the education of our young people and their educational opportunities.
[DOT] (8:00 p.m.)
Family allowances represent an education opportunity for the young. Therefore, from now on we must concentrate our efforts on them, on the young couples who also have to face more and more urgent obligations. That does not mean putting aside in any way the matter of old age pensions.
If we could do more in the field of social welfare, we would do it; if we could do more in the field of medicare, we would do it; if we could do more in the field of manpower rehabilitation, we would do it. Since it is impossible to do the maximum with regard to each piece of social legislation, it is necessary to be reasonable and to think about the other sectors of the population.
December 15, 1966

Those who are now neglected in Canada are the young couples, the young people and, from now, our demands must be directed to that social field. Let us stop making demands with regard to old age pensions only; the figures prove that we have invested and will invest in the next three years ten times more in the field of old age pensions than in the field of family allowances.
I think the time has come to be reasonable and those who are urging the government to increase to the full expenditures for old age pensions will delay social measures liable to help young Canadians. That matter cannot be considered otherwise, especially in the light of all our future social obligations during a single session.
Therefore, to show that we are well-meaning Canadians, that we are not only looking for political gains and trying to push the government into a corner and keep it from improving the lot of other groups of the population, we must instead direct our efforts towards a social program which unfortunately has been rather neglected so far and where we must catch up and where the opposition can do much to help.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, after what has been said during the past several days I had hoped that the minister and those who support this bill would come to their senses and amend it so that it would do for the old folk of Canada what they expect from it. Since last taking part in the debate I have had an opportunity to check with several old people in my area, and I failed to find one who is in sympathy with this bill except those who will qualify for the full $30, but even then they do not want to be subjected to a means test.
People across the country have no doubt that the minister is attempting to impose a means test. If the government were in touch with the grass roots it would not be long in hearing what the people think. There is no question but that this bill would have been passed several days ago had it not been for the means test.
Last July, when the minister made his first statement, he said he was going to spend $225 million. According to the last speaker on the Liberal side the $225 million has now risen to $280 million, and I have heard another figure, $270 million, quoted. Let us see what these figures mean.
We should look at this question from the point of view of paying $30 a month to 800,000

Old Age Security Act Amendment people or paying $25 a month to 1,200,000 people. In the first case the cost would come to $288 million, in the second $360 million, and the difference between paying $30 and $25 a month would be about $72 million. Added to that must be the cost of administration, which is about $5 per capita and in the case of 800,000 people would come close to $4 million. The minister's figure is $3,600,000 but my guess is that it will reach $10 million. If you take into account office space, heating, lighting, stationery and things like that for the use of people administering the means test, the cost will be another $5 million or $6 million. This would make a total of about $15 million, and such a sum would help to close the gap between the cost of giving $25 a month to all old age pensioners and the cost of giving $30 a month to 800,000.
In addition, many of these people will be paying taxes. Some of them will be pushed up into higher income brackets and a good deal of the difference, if any still exists, would be recovered in additional taxation. When all these factors are taken into consideration the total difference will probably be less than $50 million. The means test is going to be a hardship to a lot of people, and since the difference between the two schemes will be not too great I cannot understand why the government is clinging so tenaciously to its scheme which in practice will not be in the best interests of anyone.

Just give me a chance to finish and then I shall be glad to answer questions.
There is nothing sacred about the figure of $105 which the Senate committee recommended as the amount which old people needed. In many cases many of them need more; possibly many of them need less. But in trying to arrive at an equitable distribution of the increase and administration of the legislation, I say there is not one of the old folk who would not be willing to sacrifice $5 and accept the $25 figure in preference to having a means test and being required to fill out a lot of forms.
Old people may have to hire accountants to help them fill out the forms. Many of them are not skilled in the income tax regulations, and if they hire somebody the charge will probably be about $5. None of this is necessary. All the minister needs to do is make the rate uniform. The people of this country are accustomed to a uniform rate. They think in terms
December 15, 1966

Old Age Security Act Amendment of $75 and prior to that they thought in terms of $65, but always a flat rate figure without a means test. Now the minister is imposing a means test to decide who will qualify for an additional $30 a month.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
This is going to cause discontent. The result will be that persons in a neighbourhood will be pitted against one another. There will be dissension. Some of these old folk will be filling out these forms and stating that they do not have income when they do have. This will make liars out of them for no good reason whatsoever. But the Minister of National Health and Welfare has entrenched in the back of his mind the idea that this is the way it has to work in spite of what people throughout the country are saying. I say to him that if he will go out and move among these old people during the Christmas vacation he will come back with a view vastly different from that which he now holds. There is no question about that. I do not wish to continue my remarks in respect of this bill. We have discussed it at great length. The difference between the one approach and the other, in terms of money and in terms of measures such as the mini-budget which have to be brought into effect in order to pay for it, is insignificant.
This whole issue boils down to the fact that there is the one principle which the Minister of National Health and Welfare is attempting to get the old folks to swallow and the other sensible method about which they all are concerned and to which they have been accustomed for years-a flat rate. I should be pleased now to answer whatever question my hon. friend may wish to ask.

In rising to take part in this debate I cannot but think back to the days before I entered the House of Commons, the days when the Liberal party held sway in Canada and seemed almost impossible to defeat. Those were days when the Liberal party had a policy, had principles and believed in embodying those principles in the legislation which it brought forward.
In looking at this piece of legislation which has been prepared by the minister and the government I have reached the conclusion that it amounts to a reversal and repudiation of the policies which have for so long been followed by the Liberal party. I cannot help thinking of the men and women from one end of Canada to the other who took justifiable pride in a party which abolished the means test in regard to the aged citizens of this country, those who had pioneered, those who had come to this land to build their homes and bring into being a society better than the society in the countries from which they had come.

I suggest that this is a sad state of affairs in a great country like Canada which was built on individual initiative and the spirit of individual enterprise.
These old age pensioners who have a small retirement income are severely pressed by today's high living costs and have no hope of escape from this trap unless we in parliament move to intervene on their behalf. I ask the minister, why should a man or woman who has worked all his or her life, say on a railroad or in some other job, be penalized now for having earned a small pension? The government should, without question, bring in a flat $30 a month old age pension increase across the board, with no questions asked. The Senate committee on aging recommended a minimum income of $1,260 a year for all Canadians. I say, all right, let us put that into effect for everyone. But at the very least thousands and thousands of old age pensioners need some help against the cost of living, and it seems to me that the top priority item in this legislation should be some additional supplement for all senior Canadians, pegged to the rise in living costs.

I take exception to the bill, Mr. Chairman. One of the first statements the minister made was that for one to suggest a means test was involved indicated one was either stupid or dishonest. Whether you call this test a means test, a needs test, an income test or Mac-Eachen's test, the fact of the matter is that there are 50,538 pensioners in Nova Scotia in receipt of old age security payments. I suggest to the hon. member for Rosthern that the minister should not look ahead but to his derriere, because all of the actions of this government have been taken from the derriere. In suggesting that we on this side, who have tried to be constructive, have attempted to befog the issue and in standing up and repeating the words of the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace that because we believe a test is involved we are either stupid or dishonest, the minister is departing from the standard of intelligence for

Mr. Chairman, I wish to move two amendments. I will deal with them one at a time. The first is an amendment to subsection 1 of the new section 7. If hon. members will look at it they will see that it contains a limitation. The general purpose is that a guaranteed income supplement is to be paid to every pensioner commencing with the year 1967. However, by the words which follow the guaranteed income supplement will never be paid to persons born after the end of 1910. This means that persons who are now 56 years of age or older have this supplement to look forward to when they reach pensionable age, provided they qualify for it. But persons now under the age of 56 will not have this supplement available to them when they reach pensionable age no matter what their income may be.
I recognize that the plan to phase out the guaranteed income supplement is related to the time when the Canada Pension Plan benefits reach their maximum level. But there are two things to be said. First, it will never be the case that all Canadians will be covered by the Canada Pension Plan. Why, then, should we exclude from the notion of a guaranteed income level those persons who will not get benefits from the Canada Pension Plan ten years from now?
The other point is that the exclusion of such people is inconsistent, in my opinion, with the idea of increasing the basic amount of the old age security pension. This clause says in effect: we are moving toward a guaranteed income level but we are adopting it for only a limited period. If the idea of a guaranteed income is as wonderful as the minister makes it out to be, if it is to take its place with all the great pieces of social legislation about which the minister has boasted, why place it on such a temporary basis?
I shall have something to say about later clauses. I shall have other amendments to
11212	COMMONS
Old Age Security Act Amendment move in an attempt to bring about further improvements which I believe should be made in this legislation. If I could make all the improvements I wanted to make I would, for one thing, turn the supplement into part of the basic pension. In any event, if this idea is as worth while as the minister pretends, why should we have its fruits only for the next nine years and then phase them out? If the plan is such a good idea, I suggest it be permanent in its effect. I therefore move:
That clause 3 of Bill C-251 be amended by deleting from sub-section (1) of the new section 7 being enacted thereby all the words after the words "every pensioner".
If hon. members will look at the clause they will realize that this has the effect of cutting out the words "born on or before the 31st day of December, 1910." The subsection as amended would then read:
Subject to this Part and the regulations, for each month in any year commencing with the year 1967, a monthly guaranteed income supplement may be paid to every pensioner.

The resolution preceding this bill provides for "a measure to amend the Old Age Security Act, effective with respect to months beginning with January, 1967, to provide for the payment out of the consolidated revenue fund and for the charging to the old age security fund under that act of a monthly amount to be known as the guaranteed income supplement, to certain pensioners".
The expression "certain" was put in the resolution for the explicit purpose of confining the application of the measure to pensioners born on or before December 31, 1910. If that were not the purpose, Mr. Chairman, then the simple expression that has been used by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, namely, "to pensioners thereunder" would have been used. The word "certain" in
December 15, 1966	COMMONS
the resolution is a limiting word which in my judgment makes this amendment out of order.
I refer to citation 246 in Beauchesne's fourth edition which reads in part as follows:
The guiding principle in determining the effect of an amendment upon the financial initiative of the Crown is that the communication, to which the royal demand of recommendation is attached, must be treated as laying down once for all . . . not only the amount of a charge, but also its objects, purposes, conditions and qualifications.
We have qualified and conditioned the royal recommendation by including in it the expression "certain", with the intention that it would limit the application of the benefit to pensioners born on or before December 31, 1910. For that reason. I suggest that the amendment goes beyond the scope of the resolution because it widens the effect to include all pensioners and not certain pensioners as contained in the royal recommendation.

Mr. Chairman, I rise on the point of order which the minister has raised, and I suggest that this is a very serious point of order affecting the question of whether or not parliament has any rights in this field at all. We all recognize the function of a royal resolution preceding a money bill. We recognize the rules and the citations and the requirements that a bill must not go beyond the specific conditions laid down in a money resolution. But there are also citations which say that care must be taken to draft a money resolution to cover the points that the government has in mind.
There was nothing whatsoever in the resolution that perceded this bill which suggested there was to be any cut-off in terms of the date of birth of a pensioner. For the minister to stand up and make the assertions that he did tonight is for the government to say, any time it brings in a bill, that there can be no change in it because "this is what we intended and that is it".

speechtext:
Yes, I am afraid the position the minister is taking tonight is one of arrogance. He has read the resolution and I invite Your Honour to read it. I find it at page 10707 of Hansard for December 5, and it reads as follows:
That ft Is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Old Age Security Act, effective with respect to months beginning with January, 1967, to provide tor the payment out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund and for the charging to the old age security fund under that act of a monthly amount to be known as the guaranteed income supplement, to certain pensioners thereunder up to a maximum of 40 per cent of the amount of the pension payable
Old Age Security Act Amendment under that act; to provide for the determination of the income of a pensioner for the purposes of such supplement and for appeals by pensioners against decisions or determinations made under that act; and to provide for other related and consequential matters.
The resolution made it clear that there was to be a limit as to the amount. The amount could not be more than 40 per cent of the amount of the pension provided under the Old Age Security Act. It made it clear that there was to be a provision for the determination of the income of a pensioner for certain purposes and so on, but there was nothing whatsoever in that resolution that said there would be any date in the bill phasing out this plan, that there would be anything in the bill that would say that people could not get this supplement if they were born after a certain date.
For the minister to take the position that the word "certain" in the resolution covered anything the government proposed to put in the subsequent bill means that from now on, if that position is supported, all resolutions preceding money bills can be extremely simple. All the government needs to do by way of resolution preceding a money bill is to say it is expedient to introduce a measure to provide certain things. Then we will get the bill and the things in that bill will be what the government intended, and the government can say that was what was contained in the royal recommendation.
I submit that we are back to the kind of procedural debate that we had when we were on the medicare bill, when we had many arguments over what was included or not included in the royal recommendation. Surely this resolution on its face indicates that there are some things that the government felt had to be covered-the amount of the pension, the question of the test and so on, but there was no reference whatsoever to a cut-off date such as is now in the bill. Therefore I submit, no reference having been made to it in the resolution, that the government has no legal right now to claim that we cannot move this kind of amendment.
I also point out that this is not the kind of a money resolution that sets an amount of dollars in any absolute figure. When we pass legislation of this kind which provides an allowance, pension or benefit we do not say that only so many thousands or millions of dollars can be spent. We pass a bill that lays down principles, and if people meet those principles the money has to be found to meet the payments. There is no over-all ceiling on the amount of money provided. It is simply a
11214	COMMONS
Old Age Security Act Amendment matter of principle, and there was nothing in the resolution to say that one of the principles would be this cut-off date.
I submit there is more at stake in the procedural argument we are having now than just this bill. What is at stake here is the whole question of the right of the government to conceal what it has in mind when it is drafting a resolution, to say as little as possible, but by putting in that word "certain", or something like that, to be able to claim that parliament cannot make any kind of amendment. I submit, Mr. Chairman, that this point has got to be looked at very seriously, and I certainly contend that my amendment does not go beyond the terms of the resolution. As a matter of fact, my amendment accepts the alleged virtues of the resolution and says, if this is a good plan let us stay with it.
[DOT] (10:30 p.m.)
Since the minister did take some time to argue substance, perhaps I might point out again that it is no more inconsistent with the Canada Pension Plan to have an old age security provision of $105 a month or $150 a month than it is to have one of $75 a month. I suggest that argument was quite beside the point. However, I am keeping to the point of order and I contend that this amendment does not go beyond the terms of the resolution and should be allowed as in order.

If the committee will permit me to make a ruling, I am prepared to do so now. I have had an opportunity to examine the amendment in the light of the resolution. The question before the Chair is not one of substance. The question before the Chair is whether or not the amendment is correct procedurally.
I should like to read part of citation 246 of Beauchesne's fourth edition:
The guiding principle in determining the effect of an amendment upon the financial initiative of the Crown is that the communication, to which the royal demand of recommendation is attached, must be treated as laying down once for all (unless withdrawn and replaced) not only the amount of a charge, but also its objects, purposes, conditions and qualifications.
[Mr. Knowles.)
DEBATES	December 15, 1966
In the resolution reference is made to the amount of the supplement involved. In this particular case it says that the supplement is to be 40 per cent of the amount of the pension payable. Therefore in respect of that part of the resolution I do not think it would be possible to effect a change. In the amendment we have before us, however, we are dealing with limits which were not set in the resolution itself. I can understand the argument which the Minister of National Health and Welfare uses with reference to the word "certain". While I think the word "certain" does in some measure limit something, the word "certain" does not say by how much.
I should like to refer hon. members to citation 278 at page 227 of Beauchesne's fourth edition. Paragraph 4 reads as follows:
The committee is not bound by the terms of the provisions which the ministers have inserted in the bill; and, when no amount has been mentioned in the resolution, any member may propose to increase the grants specified in the bill or to extend the application of the provisions of the bill, whatever may be the cost resulting therefrom, so long as the power conferred by the royal recommendation is not exceeded.
In the recommendation which we have before us I cannot accept the view that the limitation set by the word "certain" is exceeded. May I refer hon. members also to page 799 of May's seventeenth edition. I should like to read part of the paragraph at the bottom of the page:
As, however, the power of amendment of the committee is not limited by the terms of the resolution which is before it, but by the resolution which has received the Queen's recommendation, namely the resolution by which it was appointed, it is within its powers to increase the amount, to extend the purposes and to dispense with the limitations of the expenditure actually proposed to it, so long as these changes do not extend the terms of the resolution recommended by the Queen.
It is my opinion that in the motion which we have before us the terms of the resolution preceding the bill have not been exceeded. I therefore rule the amendment in order. The hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich.

speechtext:
Certainly not. These
amendments which the minister is proposing say that income from the Canada Pension Plan is income for the purpose of the legislation. Therefore if anyone is in receipt of $60 a year or more under the Canada Pension Plan he automatically cannot receive any more benefit from this legislation. So the argument falls flat. Furthermore, during the ten year period in which this supplement is payable to the pensioners many pensioners will receive a pension during that time which will be in a much greater amount than that which will be received by people in 1977 and 1978. If the minister would study the evidence given during the hearings in respect of the Canada Pension Plan he would see that there will be hundreds and thousands of Canadians who will not receive any benefit from the Canada Pension Plan in 1976 or 1977 or maybe even by 1980. Any person who is self-employed, such as a Newfoundland fisherman, who consistently has a net income of less than $800 a year will receive no benefit from the Canada Pension Plan.
In 1961, the last year for which figures are available, there were over 101,000 Canadians who had no income whatsoever. There were over 600,000 Canadians who had an income of less than $1,000 a year. When the time comes in 1976 all these people, if born before 1910, will receive no benefit under the Canada Pension Plan and they will receive no benefit from this proposal. I am surprised at the attitude of the minister. Certainly the bill has shortcomings, but the bill would be improved
Old Age Security Act Amendment greatly if this limitation of 1910 were removed. In that way everybody would be treated the same for all time. If you wish to make another adjustment and say that in respect of the Canada Pension Plan the adjustment will be dollar for dollar, that might be an improvement if the minister wishes to accept such an amendment.
In my opinion the minister is forgetting the fact that there will be hundreds of thousands of Canadians in 1976 who will receive no benefit from the Canada Pension Plan. These are the people who will need assistance because their income will have been so low due to illness and other reasons that they will not have been in a position to set aside any savings for their retirement. These provisions such as they are should be continued without reference to the date of birth of the pensioner.

Like a number of other hon. members, I find myself completely amazed by the performance of the Minister of National Health and Welfare. Many of us do not always agree with his arguments but we normally expect some semblance of reason and logic. The only possible explanation I can think of regarding the argument which the minister attempted to advance under the guise of discussing a point of order is that he has been sitting too close to the Minister of Transport and has acquired some of the logical mania of that hon. gentleman.
The minister might have some possible ground in logic for his earlier argument if he had based it on the assumption that all of the people who would be eligible for the Canada Pension Plan would be drawing the maximun of $104 per month. speechtext:
The reaction of the Minister of National Health and Welfare to the amendment proposed by my colleague, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, demonstrates very clearly what a complete sham this so-called guaranteed income legislation is. When the minister found it necessary to do something about old age pensions, because of the pressure brought to bear not only by members on this side of the house but throughout the country, he brought in legislation to reimpose a means test on persons applying for old age assistance. In order to dress it up in high-sounding phrases the minister made speeches about a new concept in respect of pensions. He suggested that we were going to provide a guaranteed annual income. Certainly there is a great deal to be said in support of the general policy of providing a guaranteed annual income, not to be confused with the guaranteed pittance about which the minister is talking when referring to the old people of this country.
Let me remind hon. members that this is not a program to provide for a guaranteed income for everybody. As the minister has said, by the provisions of this legislation no one who reaches the age of 65 years in 1975 will be eligible for these benefits. In other words, this is simply a temporary relief measure by which the government intends to pay $30 per month to certain persons who can qualify on the basis of an income test. When


the Canada Pension Plan becomes completely effective the $30 per month provided by this measure will be phased out. This measure will not do any individual any good who reaches age 65 after 1975.
The minister says that this measure after 1975 will undermine the Canada Pension Plan and that in the next few years there will be people who will qualify for benefits under the Canada Pension Plan. If they are able to qualify for these payments they will receive them but if they cannot qualify they will not. The difference is whether they will or will not qualify by 1975.
There will be thousands of people who cannot qualify for the Canada Pension Plan. In other words, what the minister is saying is that the $75 per month old age pension is to be frozen in perpetuity. The minister has suggested that the Canada Pension Plan will help the workers of this country. This will make very little difference in five or 20 years from now because the old age security pension plan will still provide a maximum of $75 per month.

speechtext:
That is the kind of interjection that one could expect from an adolescent. If there ever was a demonstration of arrested mental development, we have just had it. I say to the Minister of National Health and Welfare that if he wants to get this legislation through with any expedition at all he should send the Minister of Transport to the Northwest Territories.
May I return to the point with which I was dealing before I was so rudely interrupted. The Minister of Transport says that there is an increase by virtue of the increased cost of living. Am I to take it then that the government says that the only increase there will ever be in the Old Age Security Act is the increase of 75 cents for each 1 per cent increase in the cost of living? Does this mean that the government never intends to give to the old people of this country any of the return that comes from increased national productivity? Does this mean that as this country increases its wealth and its production and as the general living standard rises, the old people are still to get $75 a month plus the small pittance which will be added by virtue of the fact that the cost of living has gone up? Is this all they can look forward to? This is what the government is saying, that the maximum increase for the cost of living will be 2 per cent regardless of whether the cost of living goes up 3, 4 or 5 per cent per year. The government has let the cat out of the bag. They have demonstrated that they never intended to bring down this legislation.
In the election of 1965 the government made two specific promises. One was to bring in medicare on July 1, 1967, and the other was the promise that old age pensioners would get $105 a month if they needed it. This was their program. They thought they were discharging the second commitment by bringing in the Canada Assistance Plan, and when the people of Canada and the members of the opposition made it perfectly clear that the Canada Assistance Plan based on the principle of need was unacceptable the government found it necessary to cook up some kind of legislation which would cover up their complete failure to deal adequately with old age pensions.
Old Age Security Act Amendment Instead of doing what members on this side of the house have been asking, what old age pensioners have been asking, what chambers of commerce, trade unions and farm organizations have been asking, namely, raise the old age pension to $100 or $105 a month to increase the earning power of the old people of this country commensurate with the nation's increased productivity, what did they do? They did not even have the honesty to come out and say, we are not going to give them an increased pension, we will give them a sort of relief bonus if they can pass a means test. Instead, they talked glowingly about a guaranteed annual income, and the inference was left that this was to be the beginning of a great new program of giving everybody a guaranteed annual income. This is what the press releases said and this is what the editorials said in the newspapers sympathetic to the Liberal party. This was the great step forward into a new epoch of social security, namely, a guaranteed annual income for every body. But when we see the bill it turns out that the guaranteed annual income is not granted.
